You will begin to stand outside. Strive now, in the time of mercy, because in the time of judgment the place of repentance is taken from the reprobate, which is now opened to all who seek piously. I do not know you. The light does not know the darkness, that is, does not look upon it, because if it looked, the darkness would not be.
13.26: 13.26 We ate, etc. The feasting of festivals does not help, if the piety of faith does not commend it. Knowledge of the Scriptures does not make known to God one whom the iniquity of his works shows to be unworthy. Or it is to be understood simply of the Jews, who, rejecting the mysteries of faith, think themselves pleasing to God because they feast before the Lord with victims offered in the temple and listen to the reading of the prophets. Or mystically: He eats and drinks before the Lord who eagerly receives the food of the word. In the streets, etc. Scripture in its more obscure parts is food, because it is as if broken by exposition and swallowed by eating. Drink is in the plainer parts, where it is absorbed just as it is found. They therefore testify that they have understood both the hidden and the plain, who complain, when the judge rejects them, about what they ate.
13.28: 13.28 There will be weeping, etc. Weeping is usually caused by burning, gnashing of teeth by cold, because there they will pass from the waters of snows to excessive heat. Or the gnashing shows the feeling of one indignant, who repents too late that he stubbornly did wrong. Or those who here rejoice in gluttony will gnash their teeth. The eyes will weep which here wandered through concupiscences. And note that through the weeping, which belongs to the eyes, and the gnashing of teeth, the true resurrection of the wicked is shown.
13.29: 13.29 And they will come. Many who were first fervent afterward grow sluggish. Many who were first cold suddenly catch fire. Many despised in the world are to be glorified in the future. Others glorious among men are to be condemned in the future. Or the Gentiles, who had long lived without faith, are to be called to the faith, the Jews to be cursed.
13.32: 13.32 Tell that fox, etc. The fox is a crafty animal, lying hidden in a pit for ambushes, foul-smelling, never going by straight paths. All these things fit heretics (whose type Herod holds), who try to extinguish Christ, that is, the humility of the Christian faith, in believers. Behold, I cast out demons, etc. As if he said: Neither Herod nor the heretics, whose figure he is, will be able to disturb what I intend to do. I intend, however, to cast out demons from the hearts of men, that leaving vanities they may believe in me; and to perform cures, that they may live according to my precepts; afterward I am consummated in my body, which is the Church, which, glorified on the day of resurrection, I will lead to the fellowship of the angels.
13.33: 13.33 Nevertheless I must. Herod will not be able to disturb me from acting thus and being thus consummated, nor will he be able to bring about the death of my body, which must take place in Jerusalem, where not he but Pilate rules. Today and tomorrow, etc. The first day is, by God's grace, to renounce vanities. The second, to agree with truth in conduct and life. The third is the final glorification.
13.34: 13.34 Jerusalem, etc. Where my prophets are, there I, the head of the prophets, must be sacrificed; for which sin she will justly be destroyed, and I grieve at their destruction as a loving father. How often I wished to gather. As if he said: I wished and you were unwilling; and as many as I gathered by my ever effective will, I did so with you unwilling, because you have always been ungrateful. Your children. In saying: How often I wished to gather your children, etc., he testifies that all the earlier prophets were sent by him. As a bird, etc. Beautifully, having called Herod, who was planning his death, a fox, he compares himself to a bird, because the deceitful fox always sets ambushes for birds.
13.35: 13.35 Your house. The temple or the city, because, the Lord having been killed, the Romans, plundering as it were an empty nest, took away both the place and the nation. You will not see me, etc. Unless you do penance and confess me the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face at the second coming. Until you say, etc. The crowds indeed said this to the Lord when he came into Jerusalem. But because Luke does not say that the Lord afterward returned to the Galileans so that this was sung to him by them, he compels this to be understood mystically of the coming in glory.
14.1: 14.1 And it came to pass, etc., water, whence dropsy, a watery disease under the skin, born of a fault of the bladder with swelling bloat and foul breath. And it is proper to the dropsical person that the more he drinks the more he thirsts, and therefore he is compared to one weighed down by an overflowing flux of carnal pleasures, and is compared to the avaricious rich man.
14.3: 14.3 Is it lawful, etc. Jesus teaches and works especially on sabbaths, not only on account of the spiritual sabbath but also on account of the more crowded assembly of the people, seeking the salvation of all.
14.4: 14.4 But they were silent. Rightly they are silent, who see that whatever they had said would be against them. For if it is lawful, why do they watch? If it is not lawful, why do they care for their animals? But he himself. Therefore he heals the dropsical man before the Pharisees, and soon argues against avarice, in order to convict them of the avarice by which they violate the sabbath and interpret the law badly. For on the sabbath one must rest not from good works but from evil ones, whence it is said: You shall do no servile work on it (Lev. 23), that is, sin. So in eternal rest one will cease only from evil things, not from good.
14.5: 14.5 Which of you. With a fitting example he resolves the question, to show that those who accuse him of violating the sabbath in a work of charity are themselves violating it in a work of greed. An ox into a pit. Fittingly he compares the animal that fell into a pit to the dropsical man, because he was perishing from a harmful humor. And well does he name the ox and the ass, to signify either the wise and the dull, or both peoples, namely the Jew pressed under the yoke of the law, and the Gentile tamed by no reason, but stupid and brutish, all of whom he draws out from the pit of concupiscence into which they had sunk: For all have sinned and need the grace of God (Rom. 3).
14.7: 14.7 And he spoke. After he had convicted them of avarice and violation of the sabbath, he begins to teach about the Gospel grace those present who were fit, inviting them to humility against the pride which the Pharisees had in the law, or aiming in his teaching at how they ought to choose their places at table in the Church.
14.8: 14.8 When you are invited: When, called by the preacher through the grace of faith, you have joined yourself to the members of the Church, do not exalt yourself above the rest as though higher, glorying in your merits. Lest perhaps one more honorable. He gives place to the more honorable one invited afterward who, made more secure by confidence in his own way of life, is quickly outstripped by the agility of those who have followed Christ. And with shame you take the lowest place, etc., when, recognizing better things in others, he humbles whatever high opinion he had formed of his own work, saying with the Prophet: But being exalted, I have been humbled and troubled (Ps. 87).
14.9: 14.9 And then you will begin, etc. And then, blushing that you once presumed greater things about yourself, you will begin to be humbled in penance and to know yourself to be of lesser merit, lest you now begin to seek what is kept for you at the end, because the inheritance that is hastened for at the beginning will fail in the last blessing.
14.10: 14.10 Then you will have glory, etc. Daily the Lord, while he visits and judges his guests, bestows such gifts of his Spirit on the humble that the company of the faithful glorifies them with admiration, and, astonished, bursts forth in praise of their author, saying: But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honored (Ps. 138).
14.12: 14.12 And he said. According to the order of the letter. After he warned the invited how they ought to recline at table, he warns also the inviter whom he ought to invite, lest the temporal expense of goods which he makes go for nothing, or perhaps increase sin; but let him so spend temporal things that through them the way to eternal things may lie open. And to him who had invited him. He speaks to the leader of the Pharisees, who perhaps could grow proud because he had called so many to the banquet as if out of mercy; or, as can be gathered from the Lord's words, he had invited rather that he might be invited in return, and so no special reward would follow. Do not call your friends. That brothers, friends, and the rich hold banquets for one another he does not forbid as a crime, but shows that it does not avail for the rewards of life. There are also certain banquets of such rich men which receive not only recompense in the present but also condemnation in the future; hence the Apostle: Not in revelings and drunkenness (Rom. 13), that is, in luxurious banquets, which are either held by contributions from all or are usually given in turns among companions, where no one is ashamed to do or say anything dishonorable. Lest perhaps. As if to say: If you intend to invite in order to be invited, you can be deceived there; but if you distribute to the poor, you are not deceived about the reward.
14.13: 14.13 Call the poor. He who calls the poor will receive a reward in the future. He who calls friends and brothers and the rich has received his reward. But if he does this for God's sake, after the example of Job's sons, like the other duties of brotherly love, he who commanded it himself rewards. He who calls the luxurious for the sake of wantonness will not lack punishment.
14.14: 14.14 At the resurrection. Although all are to rise, yet the resurrection of the just is spoken of singularly and as though specially their own, since they are to be changed in it.
14.15: 14.15 When he heard these things, etc. Enticed by the sweetness of the resurrection he had heard of, he bursts into its praise and asserts that those in it will be truly blessed, even if he does not well understand by what merits that blessedness can be attained. Blessed, etc. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (John 6). If anyone, perfectly incorporated by the sacrament of the incarnation, has deserved to enjoy the vision of the divine majesty, he will rejoice in eternal blessedness. But because many receive by faith only, as though in prayer, yet disdain to attain its sweetness truly, their sluggishness is rebuked.
14.16: 14.16 A certain man, etc. The incarnate Word has prepared the fullness of inner sweetness for many, but few come, because many who are subject to him through faith continually contradict him by living badly. A great supper. This banquet is called not a lunch but a supper, because after the lunch of which Matthew speaks, the supper remains; after the supper no banquet remains: from the lunch many are cast out, from the supper no one.
14.17: 14.17 And he sent his servant. The hour of the supper is the end of the age; hence the Apostle: We know on whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10). At this end the servant is sent, that is, the order of preachers, to those invited through the law and the prophets, that, with disdain put aside, they might prepare themselves to taste the supper, because all things are now ready. For with Christ sacrificed, the entrance of the kingdom lies open.
14.18: 14.18 And they began, etc. They make excuses because the kingdom is closed to no one unless the profession of his own voice excludes him. Everyone excuses himself who loves earthly things more than heavenly, even if he says he is tending toward heavenly things. I have bought a farm. The farm, that is, earthly substance. He goes out to see the farm who thinks of external things alone on account of substance, and this is what is first sought by lovers of the world, namely the substance of the body. AUGUSTINE. In the farm that was bought, lordship and pride are noted. For to have a farm, etc., up to love of earthly things is birdlime for spiritual wings. I ask you. While he says: I ask you, have me excused, humility sounds in the voice while he scorns to come, pride in the action.
14.19: 14.19 Yokes of oxen. The five yokes of oxen are the five senses of the body, which are rightly called yokes, as they are doubled in each sex; since they know and touch not the inner but only the outer things, curiosity is rightly signified by them, which, while it investigates outwardly the life of its neighbor, does not know its own inmost. And the mind of the curious person, the more expert it is about another, the more ignorant of itself. Nor do the words of the one excusing himself disagree with the signification of his vice, when he says: I go to try them. For trying usually pertains to curiosity.
14.20: 14.20 I have married a wife. Because many take wives not for fruitfulness but for the desires of the flesh, the pleasure of the flesh is signified by this item, on account of which the fastidious man refuses to come to God's supper.
14.22: 14.22 It is done, etc. Many such persons from among the Jews we have gathered to your supper, but these do not fill the place of your banquet; there remains room where the multitude of the Gentiles may be received.
14.23: 14.23 Go out into the highways and hedges, etc. Note that in this third invitation it is not said: Invite, but Compel to enter. For those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected from the desires of the present life, do not enter except compelled. Some, however, are called and despise it, who receive the house of understanding but do not fulfill it in work. Some are called and come, who fulfill in work the understanding received.
14.25: 14.25 And great multitudes went with him, etc. The crowds who follow Jesus as he journeys to Jerusalem signify those who come invited or compelled to the supper, and with their whole intention imitate Jesus, who goes before them to the vision of eternal peace. He instructs them, therefore, how those who desire that homeland with sincere love ought to renounce for its sake the affections of carnal piety.
14.26: 14.26 If anyone comes. We can both hate and love at once: so that we love those joined to us by kinship, and by the divine precept, and yet, those whom we endure as adversaries in the way of God, know how to hate and flee. Yet. Then we rightly hate the soul when we do not acquiesce in its carnal desires but resist and break them.
14.27: 14.27 And he who does not carry. The cross is carried in two ways: when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for the neighbor. And comes after me. For someone may lacerate his flesh for vain glory, or sympathize carnally with his neighbor so as to favor his fault; he seems to bear the cross, but does not follow God.
14.28: 14.28 For which of you. After the Lord had given to those following him to Jerusalem lofty precepts about contempt of the world and the abjection of the body, he adds a precept about perseverance, for which patience with humility is necessary. And this by the likeness of a builder. To build a tower. Because he gave lofty precepts, he adds the comparison of building up a height. He counts the cost. He counts the cost who discerns that temporal money must be spent, the heart turned away from the desires of the world, and the soul prepared against the adversities of the world.
14.29: 14.29 All who see. As the Apostle says: We have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men (2 Cor. 4). And in everything we do, we ought to consider the hidden adversaries who lie in wait for our works, and unless we watch against them, we suffer as mockers those whom we have as persuaders to evil.
14.31: 14.31 Or what king, etc. After the likeness of the tower to be built, he adds the likeness of a greater matter, of a king about to fight. In this it is shown that no one can reach glory by fulfilling the preceding commandments unless the sentence of the severe judge is tempered by mercy. For in the sight of God every man is imperfect. If he can. As though he meets God with ten thousand, he who offers the works of the ten commandments which he performed outwardly. But God opposes him as with a doubled number, since, finding him hardly prepared in the work alone, he examines him at once on work and thought. And therefore, while he is still far off through the delay of the judgment, we, attending to the insufficiency of our frailty, ought to send ahead, to obtain the peace of the severe judge, an embassy of tears, of good works, and of pious affections.
14.33: 14.33 So therefore, etc. He draws a conclusion from the preceding similitudes. Since he cannot build well who does not count the cost, nor meet the enemy safely who does not send ahead an embassy, therefore neither can he be my disciple who does not renounce all things.
14.34: 14.34 Salt is good. Truly, whoever wishes to be my disciple must renounce all things, because so he will be good salt, that is, worthy to be placed in the number of the apostles, to season the hearts of hearers with spiritual wisdom.
14.35: 14.35 Nor for the dunghill. Salt makes land barren. Hence the anger of conquerors sowed destroyed cities with salt, so that no seed would spring up in them. So the apostles, the kingdom of sin destroyed, restrain the seed of vices. Salt seasons foods and dries flesh. Preaching preserves human nature unharmed for its Creator from the worms and rot of vices.
15.4: 15.4 What man of you, etc. You had learned above to renounce negligence, avoid arrogance, take up devotion, not be held by worldly occupations, and not prefer perishable things to lasting ones. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm step on the great slipperiness of the world, the physician shows there a remedy even against error, namely, that the judge does not deny hope of pardon. A hundred sheep. Because the number one hundred is perfect. God had a hundred sheep, that is, a perfect number, when he created the substance of angels and men; but one perished, when man, by sinning, abandoned the pastures of life: therefore, because the number of the rational creation was diminished by man's perishing, he seeks man on earth so that the sum may be made whole. Does he not leave. As if to say: You murmur because I receive sinners, but I did not come except to gather the wandering, just as each of you labors to bring back a wandering sheep.
15.5: 15.5 He lays it on his shoulders. He placed the sheep on his shoulders who, taking human nature, himself bore our sins: hence the shoulders of Christ are the arms of the cross; there he laid down our sins, and on the neck of that noble gibbet he rested.
15.6: 15.6 And coming. Man having been restored, the shepherd returns to heaven and there finds the choirs of angels. They are friends, because in their steadfastness they continually keep his will; and neighbors, because they enjoy the brightness of his vision. And note that he does not say: Rejoice with the sheep that is found, but with me, because his joy is our life.
15.7: 15.7 I say to you. By the ninety-nine the number of the just is understood; by the one sheep, of sinners. Joy. The angels, being rational, rejoice over man reconciled to them, which kindles us to uprightness: let us do what is pleasing to those whose patronage we ought to desire and whose offense we ought to fear. More than over. If the angels are understood in the ninety-nine just who have not strayed and have no need of repentance, it seems greater to justify the wicked than to create and preserve the just, because although both are of equal power, this is of greater mercy and greater joy.
15.8: 15.8 Or what woman. The woman, that is, the wisdom of God, had ten drachmas when she created men and angels in her image. But she lost one when man withdrew from the likeness of the Creator. But the wisdom of God lit a lamp to search when she appeared in the flesh, because a lamp is light in a clay vessel, that is, the Word in flesh. When this shone among men, she overturned the house, because she disturbed the consciences of men about their guilt, and so the drachma is found, when the likeness of the Maker is restored in man. Having ten drachmas. The nature of angels and men, which the Lord willed to stand firm unto eternity, he created in his likeness. The woman therefore had ten drachmas when man was added to the nine orders of angels, that the tenth number of the elect might be completed. He did not perish from the Creator even after the fault, because the wisdom of God, shining in the flesh with miracles, restored him by the light of the clay vessel. She calls together. Her friends and neighbors are the heavenly powers, who are as near to so great a God as they contemplate him more closely. She calls them when, by the display of grace bestowed on men, she kindles them more vehemently to love of herself.
15.11: 15.11 A certain man. With the two preceding parables he suggests how much he himself rejoices with the angels over the salvation of the penitent. In this third he shows not only the joy but also rebukes the murmuring of the envious.
15.12: 15.12 And he said, etc. As God has no other from whom he is formed, by whom he is denied, so this one wishes to use his own power, that he may live with no one forming and no one ruling him. Father, give. Half the patrimony is given to those who ask, nor is it the fault of the father who gives to the younger. In the kingdom of God no age is weak, nor is faith burdened by years, unless the petitioner himself has judged himself unfit. If this one had not departed from his father, he would not have known the hindrance of age, but having set out in a far country, he rightly squanders the patrimony. And he divided. To the faithful he imparted the protection of his grace, which they desired; to the unfaithful he granted only the gift of natural ability, with which they were content.
15.13: 15.13 Not many days after. Not long after the establishment of the human race, it pleased the soul to carry free will with it, as a certain power of its nature, and to desert him by whom it was made, trusting in its own strength. And it consumes these powers the more quickly the more it deserts the giver. This is the prodigal life, which loves to pour itself out and range about in external displays, leaving him who is more inward to it.
15.14: 15.14 And he himself began. Because nothing is enough for prodigal pleasure, because pleasure always has hunger for itself; he rightly is in want who left the treasures of wisdom and the height of heavenly riches.
15.15: 15.15 To one of the citizens. That one of the citizens is he who, set over earthly concupiscences by the merit of his wickedness, is called the prince of this world. He sends him to the farm, because he subjects him to the desire of worldly substance. He feeds swine when he does the things in which unclean spirits delight. To feed swine. The swine is an unclean animal which delights in filth; so the devil, who feeds on the blood of cattle in idols and on the death of man himself. He sent him therefore to the farm, that is, made him his servant, to feed swine, sacrificing his soul to him.
15.16: 15.16 And he desired. The food of demons is drunkenness, fornication, and the like, which are enticing and provoke to their use. Nor is there any other care for the luxurious but to fill their belly, whose god is the belly (Phil. 3). But with these he cannot be satisfied, because pleasure always has hunger for itself. No one gave to him. Because when the devil makes someone his own, he no longer provides him with abundance of vices, knowing him already dead.
15.17: 15.17 How many hired servants. Those who strive to do worthy works with a view to future reward are refreshed by the daily nourishments of heavenly grace. But he perishes with hunger who, outside the father's house, that is, living without faith, seeks the blessed life in empty philosophy.
15.18: 15.18 Father, I have sinned. Although God knows all things, he nevertheless awaits the voice of confession. Without danger you may reveal what you know is already known: you have a reason for Christ to intercede for you, and that he did not die for you in vain; the Father too has a reason to forgive, because what the Son wills the Father also wills.
15.19: 15.19 Make me, etc. To the affection of a son, who does not doubt that all that is the Father's is his own, he does not presume to aspire, but desires now the state of a hired servant, to serve for wages; yet he testifies that not even this can he merit except by the father's condescension. AMBROSE. There is a distance between a servant, a hired servant, and a son. The servant, etc., up to what after the father's kiss he most nobly disdains.
15.20: 15.20 But while he was still far off, etc. Before he understood God, but when he was already devoutly seeking him, though not yet worthy by works to return, through the incarnate Word he anticipates the son's return. He came to earth before the son came to the house of confession, not forsaking the Word itself, but condescending in the Word as far as our pilgrimage. He humbled the arm, that is, the Son, for the embrace of the one returning. The Father fell upon the son's neck, while he placed on him the light yoke of his love, and kissed him, so that what is said elsewhere might be shown: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth (Cant. 1). Returning, he receives the kiss of charity from the father, while through grace he is assured of pardon.
15.22: 15.22 Bring quickly, etc. The first robe is the garment of innocence, in which the first man was made, but after the fault he knew himself naked and took a skin garment, that is, a mortal garment. A ring. That is, the seal of faith, by which the promises are sealed in the hearts of believers. On his hand. That is, in operation: that faith may shine through works, and works be strengthened through faith. And shoes. That is, the examples of those before, fortified in the office of preaching, that work may be adorned by good living, and the course prepared toward eternal things.
15.23: 15.23 Bring the calf. Preach Christ and make known his death, that one may believe in the heart, imitating the slain one, and receive with the mouth the sacrament of the passion for amendment.
15.24: 15.24 And they began to feast. Not only the son for whom the calf was killed is refreshed, but also the father and his servants, because the refreshment of God and of the saints is the salvation of sinners. And note that after the robe, ring, and shoes were given, the calf is sacrificed, because unless one has put on the hope of the first immortality, unless one has fortified works with the ring of faith, unless one has preached the faith itself by confessing it, he cannot take part in the heavenly sacraments.
15.25: 15.25 Now his elder son, etc. The son, that is, the people of Israel, who had not strayed far enough to worship idols. Nor was he in the house, because he did not penetrate the inner parts of the law: content with the literal sense, doing earthly things, expecting earthly things. This is he who bought a field and five yoke of oxen, pressed by the burden of the law, enjoying earthly senses, and married a wife in the affection of the flesh. And when he came. The son draws near the house when someone in that people, understanding the law spiritually, disapproves the labors of servile work and considers the liberty of the Church. He hears music and dancing, that is, those full of the Spirit preaching the Gospel with harmonious voices. He calls one of the servants when he takes up one of the prophets to read. And he asks him, while he examines in him what these feasts of the Church are in which he sees himself not to be.
15.26: 15.26 He asked. And now Israel asks why God rejoices in the taking up of the Gentiles, and through envy does not know the father's will, and stands outside, although he is entreated by heralds.
15.28: 15.28 He was angry. The Jews were indignant and complained because Jesus feasted with the Gentiles. And still they are indignant at the salvation of the Gentiles and do not wish to go in. But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, the father will go out to entreat Israel, when the calling of the Jews will be manifest.
15.29: 15.29 Behold, so many years. JEROME. Having followed the righteousness of the law, he is not subject to the righteousness of God. For what is greater righteousness of God than to forgive the penitent? Your commandment, etc. As though it were not a transgression to envy another's salvation, or to boast of one's own righteousness.
15.30: 15.30 You killed the calf for him. They confess that Christ has come, but through envy are unwilling to be saved. So of Jew and Gentile. But it can be taken generally of the just man and the sinner. He devoured his substance, etc. The harlots are the superstitions of the Gentiles, with whom he squanders his substance who, having left the marriage with the word of God, fornicates with the demon in foul desire. Son, you are always, etc. He does not rebuke him as a liar, but approving his perseverance with himself, and inviting him to the enjoyment of a greater exultation. All that is mine, etc. In eternal blessedness, both each of all things and all of each.
16.1: 16.1 To his disciples. Because the proud and avaricious Pharisees denied money to the needy just as they denied pardon to those who asked, therefore the Savior now speaks words about piety, sometimes to them, sometimes, with them listening, to the disciples. A certain man. A steward properly is the keeper of a farm, but here it is put for the manager, that is, the dispenser who administers the whole substance of the house. In this dispenser we are not to take everything for imitation, namely that we act fraudulently toward God. But on the contrary these similitudes are given so that we may understand that if one who acted fraudulently could be praised by the Lord, how much more pleasing to God is the one who does those works according to his command.
16.6: 16.6 A hundred barrels. The cadus in Greek is called amphora in Latin, containing three urns. The measure is filled with thirty modii. It can be taken simply thus: whoever relieves the poverty of a poor man, either by a half or by a fifth part, is to be rewarded with the reward of his mercy.
16.8: 16.8 And the Lord praised. If the dispenser of the mammon of iniquity is praised by the voice of the Lord because from unrighteous wealth he prepared righteousness for himself, and though he suffered loss, he yet praises his prudence, not because he acted fraudulently against his master but because he acted prudently for himself: how much more will Christ, who can suffer no loss and is inclined to clemency, praise the disciples if they are merciful toward those entrusted to them. Children of this world. Whoever does the works of something is called its child; hence: children of this world, that is, of darkness; and children of light, of eternal life.
16.9: 16.9 Make for yourselves. Mammon in the language of the Syrians means riches of iniquity, because they are gathered from iniquity. If then iniquity well dispensed is turned into righteousness, how much more do the banquets of the divine word, in which there is no iniquity, raise the good dispenser to heaven.
16.10: 16.10 He who is faithful. In money, to be shared with the poor. And in a greater. Clinging to the Creator and made one spirit with him. But he who does not well dispense the temporal things he possesses empties for himself the glory of eternal things over which he swells.
16.11: 16.11 If therefore, etc. He who does not give to his brothers for their use what was created by God for all will be unjust in dividing spiritual money, so that he divides the Lord's teaching not according to need but according to persons.
16.12: 16.12 And if in another's. If you do not well dispense carnal riches which slip away, who will give you the true and eternal riches?
16.13: 16.13 No servant. Rebuking avarice, he says that lovers of money cannot love God; he who loves God therefore despises money: for one cannot love transitory and eternal things at once. Or he will cling to one. AUGUSTINE. He will not indeed love. For no one loves, etc., up to and flatters himself about his goodness and impunity. You cannot, etc. He does not say to have riches, but to serve. He serves who guards as a slave; but he who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes as a master. He who serves mammon serves him who, by the merit of his perversity, is called by the Lord the prince of this world, set over these things.
16.14: 16.14 Now they heard. The Lord was warning the scribes and Pharisees not to think proudly, not to presume on their own righteousness, but to receive penitent sinners, and to redeem by alms the sins which might happen to befall them. But they deride the teacher of mercy, humility, and thrift, as if he were commanding harmful things that are less useful and should never be done, or at least useful things, but, being superfluous, urging on them what they had already perfected.
16.15: 16.15 And he said, etc. While you despise sinners as weak and despairing, and believe yourselves perfect in all things and free of all frailty, you think you have no need of the remedy of alms. But how justly this height of swelling is to be condemned, he sees who illumines the hidden things of darkness and makes manifest the counsels of hearts.
16.16: 16.16 The law and the prophets. They derided him as he argued against love of money, as if he were contrary to the law and the prophets: though in the law many rich men pleased God, and the law promises the goods of the earth to its observers, to which he replies by teaching that there is a distance between the law and the Gospel: because in the law lesser things are commanded to the carnal for the sake of the earth, and in the Gospel greater things are commanded to the spiritual for the sake of heaven. And everyone. Great is the force when, from the groaning of the earth, one seeks to possess heaven by virtue, which he could not hold by nature, when he even despises the tongues of those who deride, as the Lord was mocked by the Pharisees. Everyone who uses force hastens with vehement zeal and does not grow slack with sluggish affection. There is therefore a religious violence of faith, and a criminal slothfulness. Let us then do violence to nature, that it may not sink to earthly things but raise itself to the heavenly.
16.17: 16.17 It is easier. Although I say, The law and the prophets until John, yet I do not preach the destruction of the law: because it is easier for the greatest elements of the world to pass away than the least precepts of the law, since even those which seem light or superstitious are not empty of spiritual sacraments, when all things are recapitulated in the Gospel.
16.18: 16.18 Everyone, etc. AMBROSE. Not every marriage is from God. For Christian women are not joined to Gentiles, since the law forbids it. Where there is an unequal marriage, the law of God is not.
16.19: 16.19 A certain man. Against the avaricious mockers he confirms by an example what he had proposed, namely that the rich man is tormented in hell who did not make Lazarus a friend for himself, by whom he could be received into eternal dwellings; and it seems more a narrative than a parable. Who was clothed in purple, etc. GREGORY. Purple is the color of royal dress, from sea shells, etc., up to because he did not know the bowels of mercy, because he was unwilling to redeem his sins by the price of commandments.
16.20: 16.20 And there was a certain. If we see anything blameworthy in the poor, we ought not to despise them, because perhaps the medicine of poverty cures those whom weakness of character wounds. Full of sores. The fastidious rich man shrinks from his sores, lest amid costly feasts and perfumed guests he have to bear the stench of ulcers licked by dogs.
16.21: 16.21 Desiring. In one matter two judgments of God are fulfilled: from the sight of the poor man a heap of condemnation is brought upon the unmerciful rich man; and again from the sight of the rich man the poor man, tempted daily, is proved, whom for his greater testing poverty and sickness together, and the sight of the rich man's abundance, and no comfort given him, afflict. Dogs. In the tongue of the dogs can be signified the tongue of flatterers who lick wounds, while with dishonest favor they praise the evils which we ourselves reprove.
16.22: 16.22 Into Abraham's bosom. Abraham's bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, in which they are received after this life. The burial of hell is the depth of the punishments which devours the proud and unmerciful after this life. And was buried. In the law, not holding on to riches but plunder is condemned; in the Gospel, the rich man is tormented because he did not give of his own.
16.23: 16.23 And lifting up. The unbelievers see from afar, when, placed in the depths before the day of judgment, they look up at the faithful above them in rest, whose joys they cannot afterward contemplate. What they behold is far off, because they do not attain it by merit. He saw Abraham. GREGORY. It is to be believed that before the retribution of the final judgment the unjust, in the rest, etc., up to and are tormented by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.
16.24: 16.24 That he may dip. He who gave Lazarus no crumbs falling from the table desires water to drip from the tip of his finger into his mouth, and he who gave the least things in life seeks the least things in hell.
16.25: 16.25 Because you received. AUGUSTINE. Note that this rich man had something good, from which he received transitory good in this life, and Lazarus had something evil, but want purged it like fire.
16.26: 16.26 And in all these. As the reprobate wish to pass from punishments to the glory of the saints, so the just through mercy wish in mind to go to those placed in torments, to free them; but they cannot, because the souls of the just, although in the goodness of their nature they have mercy, yet being joined to the justice of their author, are bound by so great rectitude that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.
16.27: 16.27 I ask therefore. After hope for himself is taken from the one burning, the mind runs back to his relatives, because his punishment at times uselessly instructs the mind of the reprobate to charity, so that even then they love their own spiritually, who here, while they loved sins, did not love even themselves. There is kept for the rich man, therefore, for punishment, both the knowledge of the poor man whom he despised and the memory of the brothers he left, so that he may be tormented the more by the sight of the glory of the one despised and by the punishment of those uselessly loved. That you send. This rich man begins to be a teacher too late, when he has now neither time for learning nor for teaching.
16.31: 16.31 If Moses. Those who despise the words of the law will fulfill the precepts of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, the more hardly the more subtle they are, and him whose sayings they refuse to fulfill, they undoubtedly refuse to believe.
17.1: 17.1 And he said to his disciples. It must be known that while the Lord was speaking of mercy, the avaricious Pharisees persisted in derision, in which they caused scandal to weak hearers, lest they pay attention. These therefore he rebukes, speaking to the apostles, namely that they, by their own fault, caused scandals to come of themselves which could not fail to come in a world most full of troubles and errors.
17.2: 17.2 If a millstone, etc. According to the custom of the province where this was the penalty for crimes, that with a stone tied on they were sunk into the deep. And truly it is more useful for an innocent man to end his life by the gravest punishment than, by harming a brother, to mourn an eternal death. Of these little ones. Little not in age but in faith and spirit, who seek occasions for being scandalized; therefore you must take counsel for them, lest on your account they fall away from faith and salvation.
17.3: 17.3 Take heed to yourselves. He suggests in what order we may avoid scandals and escape the perpetual woe. If we take heed not to harm anyone, if we rebuke the penitent with zeal for justice, if we forgive from the heart the penitent, we are not commanded to forgive indiscriminately the one who sins, but the one who does penance. First, therefore, one must rebuke the sinner, that afterward we may forgive the penitent. For he who sees a sinner and is silent sins just as he who does not pardon the penitent. And if he repents. In one way we are commanded to give pardon to a penitent brother, in another to an enemy who persecutes. To a brother, by granting remission, we communicate in fellow charity; to the persecutor, who wishes us ill or, if he can, does it, we wish good things and do what we can.
17.4: 17.4 Seven times. Totality is usually designated by the number seven. It is therefore commanded that all sins be forgiven, or that one always forgive the penitent.
17.5: 17.5 Increase. Since above, Luke 16, he had said: He who is faithful in the least, etc., the apostles, who had been faithful in another's and in the least, that is, in contempt of earthly things, ask that faith be increased in what is their own and greater, so that those who from faith already have the beginnings of virtue may advance in it until they come to perfection.
17.6: 17.6 To the mulberry tree. By the mulberry, of blood-red color, whose fruit and shoots are red, the Gospel of the cross is expressed, which through the faith of the apostles was uprooted from the nation of the Jews (in which, as in the stock of the race, the word of preaching was held) and transplanted into the sea of the Gentiles, to which the parable subjoined about the ministers of the word also fits. The leaves of the mulberry, laid before a serpent, bring death, and the word of the cross, as it confers all that is saving, takes away all that is harmful. The fruit of the mulberry is white in the flower, ruddy when formed, black when ripe: so the devil, in the flower of angelic nature and the power of the glowing one, by transgressing bristled with terror at the odor, which is shut out through faith.
17.7: 17.7 But which of you, etc. The servant plowing or feeding is the teacher of the Church, of whom it is said: No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9). And the Lord says to Peter: Feed my sheep (John 21). The servant returns from the field when, the work of preaching interrupted, as if returning to the court of conscience, he reconsiders his sayings and deeds; the Lord does not at once command him to pass from this life and be refreshed in eternal rest, but to prepare at home what he may eat, that is, after the labor of open speech to show the humility of his own manner of life, for God sups in such a conscience.
17.8: 17.8 And minister to me. He ministers to the Maker who, considering his nature and fearing his judgments, humbles himself concerning his own virtues. For a minister is so called from a lesser state.
17.10: 17.10 So you also. After exhorting them to the perfection of faith, through which wonderful works are done even against the nature of things, he warns that no one should glory in his works, but the more excellent faith is outwardly in virtues, the more humble the conscience should be within, because we owe obedience to the Lord by right. Unprofitable servants. If a man demands of a man who is his servant not a uniform but a manifold service, and has no thanks for it, how much more you, who without me can do nothing, ought not to practice the use of one work or labor, but always to increase the earlier things with new zeal, and not to boast that you serve well. What we ought to have done. He who came to minister and not to be ministered unto made us debtors to himself, so that, not trusting in our works but fearing his examination, having fulfilled all that was commanded, we may acknowledge ourselves imperfect as long as we are pilgrims away from God.
17.11: 17.11 And it came to pass. After the parable by which he invites to humanity and perseverance in the diverse duties of God, the ungrateful are rebuked for the benefits bestowed.
17.12: 17.12 There met him, etc. The lepers are the heretics, who, having as it were various colors in the same body, mingle various sects, now of falsehood, now of truth, in the same preaching. Since they are avoided and kept far from the Church, they have to cry out with a great cry. Who stood, etc. Those who have sinned against the Decalogue, neither loving God (of whom they think wrongly) nor their neighbor, from whom they are divided, under the number ten cry out to God and are healed, when in the fellowship of the Church they obtain the whole and true doctrine, and discuss all things according to the rule of the Catholic faith, and are free of the leprosy of the variety of lies. But one gives thanks, that is, those who remain in the unity of the Church through humility; but those who, lifted up by pride, are ungrateful to the cleanser, are nine, because through unity they fall short of the perfection of ten.
17.13: 17.13 And they lifted up their voice. Because they recognize that they have erred in the Savior's words, they call him master of salvation, and through knowledge of the master they return to the form of salvation.
17.14: 17.14 Go, etc. Whoever, cleansed by God's grace of heretical wickedness, or Gentile superstition, or Jewish perfidy, or fraternal schism, has become free of it, must come to the Church and show the true color of faith like others.
17.15: 17.15 But one. The one who returned signifies the devout humility in Christ of the one Church, which, falling at his feet and giving thanks, because with thoughts of presumption restrained it sees how weak it is, attributes no virtue to itself; the good things it does it understands as from mercy.
17.16: 17.16 And he fell on his face. He falls on his face who is ashamed of the evils he has committed. For there a man falls where he is confounded. He who falls on his face sees where he falls; he who falls backward does not see. The good therefore fall on their face, because they humble themselves in these visible things that they may be raised to the invisible; the wicked fall backward, because they fall in invisible things, where they do not see what follows them.
17.19: 17.19 Arise. He who, acknowledging his weakness, lay humbly before God, is commanded by divine consolation to rise to stronger works, and to go on growing up to more perfect things. Your faith. The faith which inclined him to give thanks, on the contrary, perfidy condemns those who are ungrateful for benefits received. Has made you well. In the preceding parable it is decided that faith ought to be increased through humility. In this one it is shown manifestly by the facts themselves that it is not merely the acknowledged reasoning of faith but the carried-out operation of faith that saves the believer.
17.20: 17.20 Being asked. They ask because, as Luke discloses below, they supposed that when the Lord came to Jerusalem his kingdom would at once be manifested. The kingdom of God does not come, etc. Because when it comes it can be observed neither by angels nor by men, as the time of the Lord's incarnation was both fixed beforehand by the prophecies of the prophets and made manifest by the proclamations of the angels, so that he was conceived, born, baptized, preaching, dying, rising, ascending to heaven, was declared by the continual accompanying signs of angels, of men, or certainly of miracles.
17.21: 17.21 For behold the kingdom. It cannot be observed, because my kingdom is not bodily, as you think, but spiritual, which has already begun by faith. The kingdom of God. Or the Lord's answer can be taken thus: The kingdom of God is within you; he who will one day come as Judge of all now also reigns in the hearts of the faithful. But when heretics disturb the Church with wicked doctrines, the faithful desire that the Lord, returning to earth for one day, if it could be, would make the truth of the faith known. But they will not see, because what has once been shown by the Gospel's brightness does not need to be confirmed by bodily vision of the Lord.
17.22: 17.22 The days will come. He did not wish to say when he would come, but said he would come, to strike all with the terror of imminent judgment, and not to bring the security of delay. You will desire. After my ascension, when, groaning in this exile of the world, you will desire to see me in my glory, a will to be praised, yet not to be fulfilled in this world. One day. Well does he say one, because in that glory, of which the prophet says: One day in your courts is better than thousands (Ps. 83), there is no interruption of darkness, nor even any memory of misery or pain. It is good to desire the presence of this day, yet not by the greatness of desire to fashion dreams for ourselves as if the day of the Lord were at hand, as he predicts some will do.
17.23: 17.23 And they will say, etc. There were some who, reckoning the courses of the ages, said they had found a certain year, day, and hour of the consummation of the age.
17.24: 17.24 For as, etc. Do not believe them, because the second coming will be sudden and so manifest that no one under heaven can be ignorant of it, because the decision of the judgment is carried out under heaven, that is, in the midst of the air.
17.25: 17.25 But first, etc. Speaking of the glory of the coming, he inserts also the passion, so that when they saw dying the one they had heard would reign, they might soften the pain of the passion by the hope of the promised brightness.
17.26: 17.26 And as it came to pass. He supports the sudden day of his coming with several examples, and he whom he had compared to lightning (quickly flying across everything) he likens to the days of Noah or Lot, when sudden destruction came upon mortals.
17.27: 17.27 They ate, etc. Marriages and foods are not condemned, since in the former the means of succession and in the latter of nature are provided, but the immoderate use of lawful things is reproved. For because, giving themselves wholly to these things, they despised the judgments of God, they perished by fire or water. Until the day. Allegorically: Noah builds the ark when the Lord gathers the faithful in the Church. He enters it when it is completed, when on the day of judgment he illumines it by his presence. But while the ark is being built, the wicked revel, and when it is entered, they are struck with eternal damnation.
17.28: 17.28 Likewise, etc. Passing over the greatest crime of the Sodomites, he recalls only those things which would be thought light or nothing, so that you may understand with what punishment unlawful things are struck, if lawful things, and those without which life is not led, done immoderately, are punished with fire and brimstone. Lot. Allegorically: Lot, which is interpreted turning aside, is the people of the elect, who, while they dwell in Sodom, that is, among the reprobate, as a stranger, turn aside from their crimes as far as they can. When Lot goes out, Sodom perishes, because at the consummation of the age the angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the just and cast them into the furnace of fire (Matt. 13).
17.30: 17.30 The Son of man. He who meanwhile, appearing, sees all things, will then, appearing, judge all things, when he sees all forgetful of his judgments given over to this age, so that they deservedly ought to be destroyed with the world which they inhabit.
17.31: 17.31 In that day. Thus far about the fact that the kingdom, that is, Christ, comes not with observation but unexpectedly: now by what sort of persons the coming itself ought to be awaited. He is on the housetop who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually as in free air. His goods in the house are the carnal concupiscences which he had formerly loved, but, seeking heavenly things, had left behind in the world, which, with judgment imminent, he must not take up again. And he who is in the field. What he had said, that he who is in the field must not turn back, lest it seem said only of those who will openly return from the field, that is, will openly deny the Lord, he shows that many, while they seem to hold their face toward what is before, nevertheless look back in mind.
17.32: 17.32 Remember. Lot's wife signifies those who in tribulation look back and turn themselves away from the hope of the divine promise, and therefore she was made a pillar of salt, because by warning men not to do likewise, she seasons their hearts that they not be foolish.
17.33: 17.33 Whoever. He who wishes to save carnal life in the world (by denying Christ) will lose it in the future; or he who seeks the eternal salvation of the soul should not hesitate to give it to the death of this present time.
17.34: 17.34 In that night. That is, in that tribulation so dark that even the elect, if possible, would be led into error (Matt. 24). Two in one bed. Namely those who choose leisure, occupied neither with worldly nor ecclesiastical business.
17.35: 17.35 The other will be left. He who, whether through human praise or any corruption, abandons the state of life in which he was trained. Of whom Jeremiah: The enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths (Lam. 1). Two women, etc. Two differences, following the circle of mobile things. They are designated in the feminine gender, because they are governed by the counsel of their superiors, as women by men, and yet they grind together in so far as they serve the uses of the Church out of their own business. But some do so only for the sake of eternal things, who have as though they had not; others for temporal things, who hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6).
17.37: 17.37 Who said to them. To those asking two things he answers one, namely that the saints are to be taken up with him; by adding another he implies that the wicked, driven from him, are to be condemned with the devil. Wherever, etc. Wherever the Lord is bodily, there the elect will be gathered, who by humbly imitating his passion are as it were filled from his flesh, whose youth will be renewed like the eagle's through the resurrection.
18.2: 18.2 A certain judge. This parable exhorts us to pray and to believe, and to presume not on ourselves but on God.
18.3: 18.3 And a widow. This widow can bear the likeness of the Church, which seems desolate until the Lord comes, who nevertheless in secret even now takes care of her. Avenge me. Although the just are admonished to pray for persecutors, yet, with justice preserved, they seek this vengeance upon the wicked: that all the wicked perish, either converted to justice or, by punishment, with the power lost which they now have against the good, as long as this very thing is expedient for the good, or in so far as they can do anything temporally. When the just desire this end to come, although they pray for their enemies, yet they are not absurdly said to desire vengeance.
18.8: 18.8 Nevertheless. I say I will take vengeance for the just, but they will be very few, because when on the day of judgment I appear in the form of the Son of man, the rarity of the just will be so great that the ruin of the whole world must be hastened, not so much on account of the cry of the faithful unjustly condemned as on account of the sluggishness of those justly to be condemned. Do you think. In the word the unbelief of doubting is rebuked; the Godhead does not hold an opinion. For he by whom all things are made knows all things, but by doubting he rebukes the hearts of unbelievers.
18.10: 18.10 Two men. Because the parable by which he invited to prayer concluded by saying that when the Judge comes, faith will hardly be found on earth, lest anyone flatter himself about a superfluous knowledge or even confession of faith, in this parable he shows more carefully that God examines not the words of faith but the works, among which humility chiefly reigns; and because the proud have not this, presuming on their own righteousness and despising the weak, as though empty of faith, when they pray they are not heard.
18.11: 18.11 God, I thank you, etc. There are four kinds of swelling: when someone supposes that the good he has, he has from himself; or if he believes it given by God, thinks it given for his merits; or when he boasts of having what he does not have; or when, others being despised, he desires to be seen as having singularly what he has. The Pharisee labored under this plague, who went down not justified, because, attributing to himself singularly the merits of good works, he set himself above the publican.
18.12: 18.12 I fast twice. Behold, the Pharisee has an eye for displaying abstinence, for obtaining mercy, for giving thanks to God, but has none for guarding humility. And what good is it if the whole city is guarded and one gap is left through which enemies may enter?
18.13: 18.13 And the publican. Being humble, he does not dare to approach, that God may approach him; he does not look up, that he may be looked upon; he presses down his conscience but lifts up his hope; he strikes his breast, exacts punishment from himself that God may spare; he confesses that God may forgive; God forgives what he acknowledges. God, be merciful. The publican praying humbly belongs to those of whom it is said: God will not avenge his elect who cry to him. The Pharisee boasting of merits belongs to those of whom it is added: When the Son of man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?
18.14: 18.14 For everyone, etc. The controversy of the Pharisee and the publican having been set forth, the sentence of the judge is given, that pride may be avoided.
18.15: 18.15 And they brought. After the controversy was told and the sentence given to the humble, infants are brought, to show that the innocent and simple age belongs to grace. The apostles rebuke them, not that they were unwilling for infants to be blessed by the Savior's hand and voice, but because, not yet perfect in faith, they thought he would be wearied, in the likeness of men, by the importunity of those bringing them. They rebuked. Perhaps this was because they first wished the people of the Jews, from whom they were according to the flesh, to be saved, but they also interceded for the Canaanite woman. They knew then the mystery that the calling of both peoples was due, but perhaps did not yet know the order.
18.16: 18.16 Let the children. Let no one forbid the sick to come to the physician. These have as yet committed nothing in the branch, but have perished in the root. Those who cannot act for themselves have committed their cause to their elders. Let the physician touch, and bless the little ones with the great (Ps. 113). For of such is. He does not say of these, but of those who have through zeal the innocence and simplicity which these have by nature, because it is not age that reigns but conduct. For virtue is not being unable to sin but being unwilling. As a child does not persist in anger, when hurt does not remember it, does not desire a woman, does not think or speak evil, so unless you have such innocence and purity of mind, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.
18.17: 18.17 The kingdom of God. That is, we are commanded to receive the teaching of the Gospel as a child. A child in learning does not contradict teachers. He does not compose arguments and words for resisting, but receives faithfully, obeys, and is quiet.
18.18: 18.18 And he asked him. BEDE. This ruler had heard that those like children are worthy, etc., up to to those who wish to be perfect, he adds: Sell all and give to the poor (Mark 10). Good teacher. Because he called him good teacher and did not confess him God or the Son of God, he says that even a holy man is not good in comparison with God. But Christ does not refuse the testimony of goodness; he excludes the goodness of a teacher apart from God.
18.19: 18.19 But he said. AMBROSE. A cunning question, and therefore a sharp answer. For the tempter, etc., up to with these words it is defined that a rich man to be merciful is against nature. You know the commandments. This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is set before us to imitate if we wish to enter the kingdom of God.
18.23: 18.23 He was rich. No rich man, that is, one trusting in his riches, will enter, as Jesus explains according to Matthew. Not those who remain rich, therefore, but those who have ceased to be so will enter.
18.25: 18.25 For it is easier. Mystically: It is easier for Christ to suffer for lovers of the world than for lovers of the world to be converted to Christ. Christ is called the camel, because, humbled of his own will, he took up the burdens of our weakness. The needle's puncture signifies the narrowness of the passion, by which passion, as by a needle, he deigned to mend as it were the torn garments of our nature, that is, to repair it after the fall. Otherwise: it is easier for the Gentile people, deformed by the hump of sins, to enter by the narrow way of life than the Jew glorying in merits and unwilling to humble himself to undergo the light burden of Christ.
18.26: 18.26 Who can? They understand that all who love riches, even if they do not have them, are to be counted among the number of the rich: otherwise, since the crowd of the poor is greater, they would not say: Who can be saved?
3.22: 3.22 In you I am well pleased. Not another's things in the Son, but his own are praised, as if he said: Whatever you have, are mine.
3.23: 3.23 About thirty years. BEDE. That he is baptized at thirty, etc., down to as in Jeremiah and Daniel.
3.26: 3.26 Who was of Mattathias, who of Amos, who of Nahum, who of Esli. BEDE. Mattathias who descends through Solomon, etc., down to who by carnal generation is shown to have been made the Son of man.
3.29: 3.29 Who was of Levi. Not however were these four who are inserted in this place sons of Jacob, but they shared their names. BEDE. As alluding in the names to what was figured in them, etc., down to that diverse kinds of virtues might go before.
3.31: 3.31 Nathan. THE SAME. That Matthew through Solomon, etc., down to to whom judgment is given by God the king: He is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.
3.37: 3.37 Methuselah. AMBROSE. The years of Methuselah are counted beyond the flood, it signifies Christ, whose life knows no age. Who was of Enoch. BEDE. Ascending from the baptized Son of God to God the Father, at the seventieth step he puts Enoch, etc., down to whom in the immutable resurrection of contemplating the wisdom of God it shows are to be joined through the ages.
3.38: 3.38 Seth. Seth, the later son of Adam, is not passed over, that, since there are two generations of the people, he may signify that Christ is to be counted in the later rather than in the earlier generation. Who was of God. The generation begins from the Son of God, ends in the Son of God, the created goes before in figure, that the born may follow in truth; the made to the image goes before, that for his sake the image may descend.
4.1: 4.1 And was led. AMBROSE. He was led into the desert with this counsel, to provoke the devil; for unless he had contended, this one would not have conquered for me; by mystery, to free Adam from exile; by example, to show us that the devil envies those tending to better things. Into the desert. Historically: in that desert which is between Jerusalem and Jericho, where figuratively he had said Adam was overcome by the devil.
4.2: 4.2 He was hungry. BEDE. It is not written of Moses or Elijah, etc., down to he hungers, however, not so much for the food of the body as for the salvation of the soul.
4.3: 4.3 If you are the Son of God. AMBROSE. He knew the Son of God was to come, but did not think he had come through infirmity of body, etc., down to he who feeds not on this word does not live.
4.4: 4.4 It is written. He teaches us to fight rather by doctrine than by miracles, by humility than by power, nothing to be done at the devil's will, nor out of regard for declaring power.
4.5: 4.5 And he led. Luke follows as the thing was done, placing covetousness in the middle, pride last, according to the manners of the present time, because pride rages after all virtues. Matthew does not follow the order of the history, but of the temptations of Adam.
4.6: 4.6 To you I will give. He says this of arrogance, not that the whole world is his, for there are some good. To me it is delivered. Power is not from the devil, but is yet exposed to the devil's snares. Nor is the ordering of powers therefore bad, because the powers are exposed to the wicked one.
4.7: 4.7 You therefore. BEDE. The devil saying to the Savior: If falling down you will adore me, hears on the contrary that he himself ought rather to adore him, his Lord and God.
4.8: 4.8 If you are the Son of God. In all the temptations he does this, to understand whether he be the Son of God. But Christ so tempers the answer as to leave it ambiguous: Cast yourself down. Whom neither gluttony nor avarice conquered, vainglory tempts, in case he might be cast down even by the very boasting of his own victory. Cast. This voice befits him who strives to hurl all down. In which he is shown weak who can harm none, unless first he cast himself down.
4.9: 4.9 It is written. Because he had put forward the example of the Scriptures, he is overcome by the examples of the Scriptures. The devil, however, uses the testimonies of the Scriptures through heretics, not to teach but to deceive.
4.10: 4.10 To his angels. BEDE. This prophecy is not of Christ, but of a holy man. Even if it were of Christ, he ought to have recalled also what follows: You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample under foot the lion and dragon, Psalm 90. But of the help of angels he speaks as to a weak man, of his own trampling he is silent as a shifter.
4.13: 4.13 And all being ended. THE SAME. Three temptations conquered, he says every temptation ended, etc., down to yet he fears to press on, lest he be too often triumphed over.
4.14: 4.14 And the fame went out. He is honored not only by those present for the miracles seen, but the fame was spread among the absent.
4.15: 4.15 He taught. After miracles behold wisdom, by which he teaches, which doctrine he magnifies by the preceding miracles.
4.16: 4.16 And he stood up to read. BEDE. He who had not come to be ministered unto but to minister, etc., down to or correct by the attestation of the reading of the prophecy.
4.18: 4.18 The Spirit. THE SAME. In the above prophecies the Savior speaking of the calling of the Gentiles and the confirmation of the Church, etc., down to because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him. To preach to the poor, etc. He understands the Gentiles who were truly poor. For they had neither the knowledge of God, nor the law, nor the prophets, nor anything else among goods, and were destitute of all other spiritual riches.
4.20: 4.20 And when he had folded. BEDE. He read to those who were present, etc., down to but according to the capacity of the hearers commits the word to the teacher to be dispensed.
4.23: 4.23 Physician. As the son of a carpenter, so with the same folly of error; they call him physician, but in their error the truth lies hid. For he was truly the son of the carpenter, who through him in the beginning made all things, who works in the Holy Spirit and fire, who in the great house of this world makes vessels of diverse kinds. He is also a physician, because through him all things that are in heaven and on earth were restored. Who says of himself: They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill, Matthew 9.
4.24: 4.24 Amen I say to you. BEDE. Not only the Lord and head of the prophets, etc., down to turns away the miracles of his power.
4.25: 4.25 In the days of Elijah. THE SAME. As if to say: It is not contrary to the example of the prophets, etc., down to because there was no abundance of knowing the divinity.
4.26: 4.26 A widow. THE SAME. The widow to whom Elijah is sent figures the Church of the Gentiles, etc., down to in which the bread of eternal life is prepared for us.
4.27: 4.27 Naaman the Syrian. THE SAME. Naaman, which is interpreted comeliness, signifies the people of the nations, etc., down to because the baptized must be confirmed by participation of the Lord's body.
4.29: 4.29 And they led him. THE SAME. The Jews worse disciples, with the devil as master, etc., down to as if kept by the hand of the divine Sculptor.
4.31: 4.31 And he went down, etc. THE SAME. Neither moved by indignation, nor offended by crime, etc., down to nor is the law dissolved if there be a renewal of man already falling.
4.33: 4.33 And in the synagogue. THE SAME. In the synagogue is a man having an unclean spirit, because he had lost the Holy Spirit. For the devil had entered where Christ had spiritually gone out.
4.34: 4.34 I know you. By works he could be proved the Son of God. But did he not say to the Apostles: Greater things shall you do? The solution: by works, that is by the manner of operation. Others said: In the name of Jesus, etc. He said: I say to you, etc.
4.35: 4.35 And when he had thrown him. BEDE. The one to be cured is allowed by the demon to be thrown into the midst, that the power made manifest may invite more to salvation.
4.36: 4.36 And in power. Not as men who cast out demons in the word of God, but he works miracles by his own power.
4.38: 4.38 Into Simon's house. The house of Peter is the circumcision committed to his apostleship. The mother-in-law is the Synagogue, which is in a way the mother of the Church committed to Peter. She has a fever, because she labored with the heats of envy, persecuting the Church. But Jesus standing over her heals, because where the fear of God begins to be, such a boiling is wont to recede.
4.40: 4.40 And when the sun was down. BEDE. The setting of the sun is the passion of Christ, through which more possessed are healed than he had healed sick when living before in the flesh, because living in the flesh he taught few of the Jews, after the resurrection he appeared to the Gentiles.
4.41: 4.41 You are the Son of God. THE SAME. When the devil saw him wearied with fasting, etc., down to because if they had known the Lord of glory, they would never have crucified him, Matthew 1.
4.42: 4.42 And when it was day. Mystically: the light of the resurrection being manifest, he is sought by the throngs of believers: and found in the desert of the Gentiles, he is held that he go not away.
5.1: 5.1 And it came to pass. Neither by time nor place is the crowd restrained from the zeal of being healed; evening presses on, and yet it follows; the lake meets them, and the crowd presses, and therefore he goes up into Peter's boat. By. BEDE. The lake designates the present age. The Lord, however, is no longer in the lake as no longer in passible flesh, but by the lake, because in that flesh in which he suffered he entered upon the stability of perpetual rest.
5.2: 5.2 He saw two ships. THE SAME. The two ships mystically signify the circumcision and the uncircumcision which he saw, because in both peoples he knew who are his, whose hearts he brings from the waves of the world to the tranquility of the life to come, as to the shore, by living mercifully.
5.3: 5.3 He asked him. THE SAME. That first he asks the boat to be put out a little from the land, etc., down to belongs to the more remote nations to whom afterwards it was preached.
5.4: 5.4 Launch out into the deep. AMBROSE. Though to others it is commanded to let down the nets, etc., down to or from the flowing gifts of the Holy Spirit the Church is instructed and armed.
5.5: 5.5 At your word, etc. BEDE. Unless by the word of grace the instruments of disputations be let down, etc., down to even amid the scandals of persecutors.
5.7: 5.7 And they filled. THE SAME. This filling grows to the end of the age, etc., down to and such humility merits the pious consolation of the Lord.
5.10: 5.10 From henceforth. THE SAME. This belongs specially to Peter himself, to whom is expounded what the catch of fishes signifies. But as then by nets fish, so by words he will sometimes catch men, in which Peter is a type of the whole Church.
5.12: 5.12 In one of the cities. Here two comings to Capernaum are noted. The first, John being imprisoned, when he continuously did those three miracles; the second, when he came down from the mountain, the apostles being chosen, when this miracle of the leper is done.
5.13: 5.13 He touched. Out of humility, to teach us to spurn no one for any bodily defilement. He touches not disdaining, commands not distrusting, applies the testimony of the work. I will. He says it against Photinus, commands it against Arius, touches it against the Manichee.
5.14: 5.14 He charged him. BEDE. He orders to be silent, and it cannot be silent. Not that he wished something and could not, but he gives an example that his own may wish to be hid in the great things they do, but that they may profit others, are betrayed against their will.
5.15: 5.15 And great multitudes came, etc. BEDE. The healing of this man draws many multitudes to the Lord. For to teach that he himself was healed within and without: the benefit received, even commanded, he does not conceal. But Mark also says, performing the evangelical office: But he being gone out, began to publish and to blaze abroad the word, Mark 1.
5.16: 5.16 And he prayed. When he prays he forms the contemplative life, when he heals the active. BEDE. He heals as God, prays as man. In the city, etc., down to that it may speak silently through inward desires.
5.17: 5.17 And it came to pass, etc. THE SAME. Where sitting he taught Luke passed over for brevity, etc., down to which not by birth but by lighting up with virtues he had made his own. And there were. AMBROSE. Among the remedies of the other weak, those coming together, etc., down to and the lame steps of our actions be reformed by the remedy of the heavenly word.
5.18: 5.18 Men carrying. Allegorically: that is, lifting up to higher things the mind of men, though torpid with the weakness of the outer man; by whose aids again it is taught both to raise and humble itself more easily before Jesus, to seem worthy of the Lord's sight. For God regards humility. And they sought, etc. BEDE. They desire to offer, but the crowd interposed shuts them out, because often the soul, etc., down to because by piety of faith one descends to the humility of Christ, and comes to the knowledge of Christ.
5.19: 5.19 And by the tiles. THE SAME. The house of Jesus is described as covered with tiles, because under the contemptible veil of letters, if there be a teacher to unlock divine things, the power of spiritual grace is found. That he is let down with the bed signifies that Christ ought to be known by man still set in this flesh.
5.20: 5.20 Whose faith. BEDE. The faith of each avails much, since through another's faith a man is saved within and without. THE SAME. This cure of the paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul sighing to God, etc., down to which are prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice. Man, are forgiven, etc. You, man, a sinner, I, God who forgive sins, who for the merit of others release your sins to you. He who is therefore burdened with sins, let him bring the Church to pray for him. Because for the fault of the soul the body also was infirm, therefore about to heal the body, he first heals the soul.
5.21: 5.21 Who can forgive? No one forgives sins but God, who through them also forgives to whom he has given the power of forgiving. Since therefore Christ forgives, he is proved truly God. They render true testimony to God, but by denying the person of Christ are deceived. For perfidy can confess, cannot believe. And so testimony is not wanting to the Divinity, faith is wanting to salvation. God, however, wishing to save sinners, shows himself God both by knowledge of hidden things and answers them with the wonder of deeds: Why do you think evil in your hearts? With the same majesty and power by which I behold your thoughts, I can forgive men their offenses. Understand from yourselves what the paralytic obtains. But because you know not spiritual grace, nor believe what was done within, let it be proved by a visible sign that it is not of less power, that in the Son of man you may know the hidden power of majesty by which he can forgive sins as God.
5.22: 5.22 And when he knew, etc. AMBROSE. The great priest saw leprosy in the hearts of the Jews, and showed them worse than that leper whom, cleansed, he ordered to offer himself to the priest. But these the high priest repudiates lest their leprosy defile others too.
5.24: 5.24 I say to you, arise. BEDE. To arise is to draw the soul away from carnal desires. To take up the bed, etc., down to by the remission of the penalty understand the remission of the fault.
5.26: 5.26 And astonishment. AMBROSE. The unbelievers behold him rising, wonder at him going away, and prefer to fear the miracles of the divine work than to believe; for if they believed they would not fear, but love. For perfect charity casts out fear, 1 John 4.
5.27: 5.27 Levi. BEDE. The same Levi who is also Matthew. But Luke, etc., down to he was changed from a publican to an evangelist. BEDE, AMBROSE. He left his own who snatched others'. Nor did he leave only the gains of the tolls, but despises also the danger which could come from the princes of the age, because he left the accounts of the tolls in disorder. And because he reserved to himself no regard or thought at all of this life, he deserved to be a faithful dispenser of the Lord's talents. BEDE. By the election of Matthew is expressed the faith of the Gentiles, who first gaped at worldly things, but now refresh the body of Christ with diligent devotion. By the pride of the Pharisees is hinted the envy of the Jews, which is tormented by the salvation of the Gentiles.
5.30: 5.30 Why, etc. AMBROSE. Every question from the law, which is tenacious of justice, has not, etc., down to and walking and all he did serve salvation. AMBROSE, BEDE. He who receives Christ into the inner dwelling is fed with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. And so the Lord enters, and reclines in the affection of him who believed. But again the envy of the perfidious is kindled, the form of future punishment is prefigured. For the faithful feasting and reclining in the kingdom of heaven, perfidy fasting will be tormented. It is shown also how much difference there is between the emulators of the law and of grace, because those who follow the law will suffer eternal hunger of mind. But those who receive the word in the interior, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly food and the fountain, cannot hunger and thirst, and therefore those who fast in mind murmur, saying: Why with publicans, etc.?
