Sons of the devil, they pour out the poison of the serpent. The serpent first sent forth his voice, saying to Eve: Why has God commanded you that you should not eat of every tree? Genesis 3. These imitate him.
5.31: 5.31 The physician. Christ the physician who, by a wonderful way of healing, was wounded for our iniquities. By this medicine the poison of the serpent is excluded. He who uses this medicine does not remain fasting.
5.32: 5.32 To call the just. BEDE. The just he calls those who, ignorant of the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, are not subject to the justice of God; and, presuming on the law, seek not the grace of the Gospel; the sinners who, attending to their evils, and not thinking themselves able to be justified by the law, submit themselves by penance to the grace of Christ.
5.33: 5.33 Why the disciples. BEDE. Matthew says the disciples themselves asked this. But it is to be known that both asked. THE SAME. Spiritually: the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, because those who the works of the law, etc., down to eats with sinners, that you may understand grace and power.
5.34: 5.34 Can you? THE SAME. As long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, neither can we fast, etc., down to then the children of the bridegroom shall fast, desiring the coming of the Judge.
5.35: 5.35 But the days will come. THE SAME. As if to say: You will do it, that mourning they fast, because you are, etc., down to as long as the Lord conversed in the flesh with the disciples. Then they shall fast, etc. Of both fastings, which is in tribulation or in joy, he answers: When the bridegroom shall be taken away, then they will be in sorrow and mourning, until by the Holy Spirit consolation be given; which gift received, the fast that is made through gladness they will celebrate, renewed now into spiritual life. And here first he deals with the fast which pertains to the humility of tribulation. That, however, which pertains to the joy of the mind (when the mind is suspended to spiritual things and therefore alienated from bodily foods) he signifies by the following similitudes, showing that for the carnal, and for this reason still drawing the old sense, this kind of fast does not suit.
5.36: 5.36 From a new garment. BEDE. To the old garment are compared the disciples, who are still the old man. To whom a new cloth, etc., down to hence the Apostle: Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, Ephesians 4.
5.37: 5.37 Wine. With wine we are refreshed within, with a garment covered without. The garment is good works which we do outwardly, by which we shine before men. The wine, the fervor of faith, hope and charity, by which in the sight of God we are reformed within in newness of sense. Into bottles. BEDE. They are compared also to old bottles who are burst by new wine, that is spiritual precepts, rather than contain it. The bottles will be new when after the ascension, the Spirit received, they will be renewed by praying with desire of his consolation. Otherwise: to the soul not yet renewed, but persevering in the oldness of malice, the sacraments of the new mysteries ought not to be committed. Otherwise: the old bottles are the scribes and Pharisees; the new cloth and new wine, the precepts of the Gospel, which the Jews cannot bear, lest a greater rent be made, with whom the Galatians mixed the precepts of the law, new wine into old bottles. They suit, however, the apostles, not those who, depraved by the traditions of the elders, cannot keep the sincerity of the precepts of Christ; hence it is added: And no man, because to the Jews steeped in the saliva of the old life the precepts of the new grace were sordid, because piled with the traditions of the elders, they could not perceive the sweetness of the spiritual words.
5.38: 5.38 But new wine. The fragility of the human condition is laid open, when our bodies are compared to the skins of dead animals. But the bottles being renewed, new wines are hired, when we keep inviolate the sacraments we have received. These bottles, if they are full, grace preserves, if empty, moth and rust consume: let them be always full.
6.1: 6.1 And it came to pass, etc. BEDE. He says that the letter of the sabbath had begun to be dissolved, etc., down to after the second, from that by which the preceding were said or done. Through the corn, etc. Mystically: the field is the world; the crop of the field, the fruitfulness of the human race; the ears, the fruit of the Church, with which the apostles are satisfied, feeding themselves on our progress. The disciples plucked, etc. The disciples, not having time to eat because of the importunity of the crowds, hungered as men, but plucking ears they console their want, which is an indication of a more austere life, to seek not prepared meats but simple foods. And note that the apostles now destroy the letter of the sabbath against the Ebionites, who receive the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law. BEDE. Mystically: the disciples hungering for the salvation of men pass through the corn, that is through regions which, etc., down to rebuking the teachers of the law as ignorant of the law.
6.2: 6.2 They said to them, etc. Others say these things were objected to the Lord himself. But they could have been objected by different persons both to the Lord and to the disciples, and whomever it was objected to, it looks chiefly to him. On the sabbaths. The sabbaths signify holidays; either those kept in this age by those at leisure for the superstitions of the Jews; or those that shall be kept in the future, when in perpetual solemnity we shall eat the good things of the earth.
6.3: 6.3 Have you not read this, etc. BEDE. How is it objected as a crime to the Lord which in a servant is not held a crime? The true king, etc., down to all the children of the Church are priests, anointed with the Holy Spirit that they may offer themselves.
6.4: 6.4 He went into the house of God. Great is the grace of hospitality, the danger of death being set before him, the mind of the priest does not decline the guest. And so we ought to transfer others' dangers to ourselves. But the true David also, priests do not exclude from the hospitality of the mind even for danger of death.
6.6: 6.6 A man. BEDE. Mystically this man signifies the human race withered in the fruitfulness of good work, through the hand stretched to the tree in the first parent, which the innocent hand stretched on the cross heals. And well was the hand in the Synagogue withered, because where the greater gift of knowledge, there the transgressor is subject to greater guilt.
6.7: 6.7 They watched. THE SAME. Because the destruction of the sabbath, which they charged in the disciples, the master excused by a probable example, now by watching the master himself they wish to calumniate, that if he do not cure they may accuse of cruelty or weakness, if he cure, of transgression.
6.9: 6.9 I ask you. BEDE. Anticipating the calumny they were preparing for him, he reproves them, etc., down to God is not the author of evil, but those whom he does not save he is said to destroy.
6.10: 6.10 Stretch forth. THE SAME. The weakness of the unfruitful soul is cured in no better order than by largeness of alms; hence it is said: Let not your hand be stretched out to receive and shut when you should give, Ecclesiastes 4. Because in vain he stretches out his hands to God to pray for sins who does not stretch them out to the poor as he can.
6.11: 6.11 Madness. Because they were moved by envy alone, for it was no fault either in the man to stretch out his hand or in Jesus to heal. It was great madness to plot the death of him by whose benefits they greatly needed.
6.12: 6.12 He went out into a mountain to pray. The mountain on which he chooses and teaches the apostles signifies the height of justice, because they were to be instituted and to preach, that they may not remain with the weak but be lifted to higher things. So the law also was given on a mountain. He brings the apostles more eminently that the mountains may first receive from the mountain the peace to be announced to the people. So also Moses, alone understanding the law spiritually, ascended the top of the mountain in which God was.
6.13: 6.13 His disciples. Of whom he chose twelve whom he named apostles, that is sent in his place; hence: As the Father has sent me, I also send you, John 20. Ascending the mountain he calls to himself, chooses whom he will, because it is not of their zeal but of divine grace that they were called to the apostleship; hence: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, ibid. 15. Not the wise, not the rich, not the noble did he choose, lest he seem to have led by prudence, redeemed by riches, drawn any to grace by authority of power and nobility.
6.14: 6.14 He surnamed. Not only first, but long before when he is said to be brought by Andrew: You shall be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter. But Luke, wishing to name the names of the twelve apostles, since he had to say Peter, wished briefly to hint that he was not called so before; but so the Lord surnamed him that it might not be thought done by chance, but by the change the sacrament of the rock might be commended to the hearers.
6.15: 6.15 Matthew. Matthew places himself below his equal Thomas in the order out of humility, though he is set before by the other evangelists.
6.17: 6.17 And coming down, etc. About to choose apostles the Lord went up into the hills; about to teach the crowds he returns to the plains, because the crowds suffice to see Christ only in the lowly, and it is rarely found that either the crowd follows the Lord to higher things, or any weak man is cured on the mountain, but the fever of lusts being quenched and the light of knowledge kindled, each step by step ascends the summit of virtues. The sea coast. Not from the neighboring sea of Galilee, because they do not put this in place of a miracle, but it is named from the great sea. In which Tyre and Sidon also could be comprehended. But because they are cities of the Gentiles, they are purposely named, that how great the power of Christ is may be intimated, which stirs up even foreign cities.
6.18: 6.18 That they might hear. If we say there are two sermons, he went up into the mountain and had disciples there; and afterward came down and made this to the crowd. If we say it was one, it is to be understood that he went up the mountain, and after a little came down and made the sermon where the plain was.
6.19: 6.19 To touch him. He touches Christ who believes faithfully in him. He is touched by Christ who is strengthened in him. He who so touches and is touched is healed by his Spirit's power.
6.20: 6.20 And he lifting up, etc. Though he speaks generally to all, specially he lifts his eyes upon the disciples, that those who with attentive ear of the heart receive the word of God may receive more widely the light of inner savor; to whom sitting on the mountain he opens his mouth to bring forth great things to them, standing on the plain he directs his eyes that they may patiently understand what is heard. Blessed are the poor, etc. Those who cannot yet climb the citadel of consummated virtue are meanwhile to be cherished with the beatitude of general perfection, that gradually advancing to better, while they gladly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may sometime ascend loftily to him sitting on the mountain. For those whose hearts he is still persisting to tame, he addresses as standing. Those whom he finds exercised by long study and already docile, to these as sitting quietly he intimates mystical things. BEDE. What in Matthew is said fully through eight beatitudes in the sermon of perfection to the apostles on the top of the mountain, this in Luke, etc., down to but because he excelled in faith, by faith above the rest he deserved the principate.
6.21: 6.21 You that now hunger. He who hungers has compassion on the hungering: by compassion he gives, by giving becomes just; he shows himself equal to inferiors, excludes guile, seeks truth. You that now weep. He who, for the riches of the inheritance of Christ, for the bread of eternal life, for the hope of heavenly joys, desires weeping, hunger and poverty is blessed; much more blessed who fears not to keep these virtues amid adversities.
6.23: 6.23 Rejoice and exult. Amid hatreds of hearts, amid reproaches of tongues, amid hands of persecutors, dwell with gladder heart, in view of the heavenly reward. According to these things. By the example of the prophets he strengthens them, because those who speak the truth are wont to suffer persecution.
6.24: 6.24 But woe, etc. Matthew on the mountain, the beatitudes only of the good; Luke on the plain, also describes the woes of the wicked, because hearers still unlearned must be compelled to good by threats and terrors, the perfect it is enough to invite by rewards. But woe. When above the kingdom of heaven is said to be of the poor: by contrast it appears that he who seeks consolation in temporal things alienates himself from this kingdom. Nor are riches so much as the love of riches in fault. Mystically: the rich Jewish people, or heretical, or the philosopher of the world, who, delighted with abundance of words and the patronage of eloquence, passing beyond the simplicity of the true faith, laid up useless treasures, disputing after the custom of the age of the generation of Christ, who in the future will recognize the poverty of their faith, and the food of perfidy which they now belch forth, wasted by eternal fast will know to be the cause of so great punishment. And there will be a time when they will mourn their laughter. To whom it is well said: Woe when men shall bless you; because while here they please the powerful, they subject themselves to perpetual curse, because as the poor hungering, weeping, are proved by the wickedness of the evil, so those given to riches, feasts and laughter, by the evil patronage of flatterers are nourished to greater punishment.
6.25: 6.25 You that are filled, etc. You who among the rich abound more, as the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted, who asks a drop of water from the finger of Lazarus. Woe to you that now laugh, etc. Solomon: The heart of the wise is where there is mourning, and the heart of fools where there is mirth, Ecclesiastes 7.; teaching that folly is to be ascribed to those who laugh, prudence to those who weep.
6.26: 6.26 When they shall bless you, etc. It is a great part of the punishment of sinners that their crimes are not only not reproved but moreover praised as well done.
6.27: 6.27 Love your enemies. Having said what they may suffer from enemies, he adds how they ought to behave toward the enemies themselves. And here the Church is not fed with milk but strengthened with the stronger food of charity. It is not enough not to hate, but what is beyond human nature is commanded, to love. And whereas the law orders reciprocity of vengeance, the Gospel bestows charity on enmities, kindness on hatreds, prayers on curses, patience on persecutors, even the grace of reward on the hungering.
6.28: 6.28 Pray for those who calumniate you. What the prophets seem to imprecate are not wishes of those desiring but predictions of things to come: for they prayed for enemies.
6.29: 6.29 And to him that strikes you. Since charity is patient, it ought to bear the patience of the striker, since it is kind it ought not to answer curses. If it seeks not its own, it ought not to resist the one robbing, if it is not envious, 1 Corinthians 13., it ought not to hate the enemy. Offer to them, etc. The physician of souls commands those whom he instructs to cure their neighbors to bear all that can avail for the salvation of neighbors. And it pertains to mercy, that as from sick and frenzied children, if their health demands it, many things be suffered until the infirmity pass. What is so wonderful as to offer the cheek to one striking? Rather the onset of every indignant one is broken, anger is calmed; and by patience he is invited to penance. The garment. What is said of garment and coat is to be done in others also, which by some right we call temporarily ours. For if this is commanded concerning necessaries, much more are superfluities commanded to be despised.
6.30: 6.30 Do not ask again. Because charity is patient, it is kind, 1 Corinthians 13.; not only does it bear injuries of the enemy bravely, but also kindly anticipates the favor of a friend, that by other benefits they may be drawn.
6.31: 6.31 And as you would. Lest he seem to dissolve the law, in benefits he keeps the reciprocity which he neglects in injuries. Nor does he say as they do, but as you would that men should do to you, do also to them, that the reciprocity may be more abundant, when the act is equal to the wishes. And not only to friends now extend the works of charity, but also to enemies, that they may begin to be friends, and first extend the affection of love, and afterward the works of charity.
6.32: 6.32 And if you love. In so far as the degree of your profession is more eminent, so far must the care of virtue be fuller, that you embrace even the unloving in the bosom of charity. There are two kinds of benefit: either when we gladly give what we give, or when we lend to one who will repay.
6.35: 6.35 But, etc. After refuting as fruitless the love and mutual benefit of sinners, he now shows how these ought to be done fruitfully by the faithful, as if to say: Though to sinners such love and mutual benefit do not profit, yet do you love, not only by the lead of nature, as they their friends, but by a higher degree of virtue your enemies. The philosophers divide justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called piety; another toward parents or the rest of the human race; a third toward the dead, that the due funeral rites be paid to them. But the Lord, surpassing the oracle of the law and the summit of prophecy, extended the office of piety to those also who have injured. Hoping for nothing thereby: and it shall be. Not fixing the hope of reward in man. Who whether he returns what you lent, God will return also at whose command you did it, or whether he does not return, your inheritance will be forever.
6.36: 6.36 Be therefore merciful, etc. He rains upon the evil, the earth denies not its yield, the same sun enlightens good and bad. Mystically: the people of the Jews he waters with prophetic rains, and the ray of the eternal sun shone on the undeserving. If therefore they believe, be merciful to them, by teaching and by lifting up, and do not rashly judge, lest anyone conscious of his own offense be forced to pass sentence on another.
6.37: 6.37 Judge not. There are certain middle and uncertain things as to the mind with which they are done, because they can be done well and ill. We know not also what he will be who now appears bad, of whose correction to despair and to rebuke him as an outcast is rash. Of manifest things which cannot be done with good mind, we are allowed to judge.
6.38: 6.38 For with the same measure. It can be taken generally of all that is done by mind, hand, tongue, because God will render to each according to his works. With the same, AMBROSE. God will not repay with unjust measure, but it is as if he said: The very rashness of judging and the unjust measure hurts you, punishes you, and often not him of whom you do this. Or if you judge and measure rightly, it profits you, saves you, though sometimes not him on whom you bestow it.
6.39: 6.39 He spoke. By which he invites to give alms and to forgive injury. Can the blind? If against the violent anger has blinded you: if against the asker you will be covetous, can you with your vitiated mind cure his vice? Not only he who did you injury but you also who know not how to bear it shall be guilty. But if his wickedness finds you tranquil, he will repent, and you will be crowned for patience, because you took care to lead the blind man by the seeing eye, that is a serene heart, to the light.
6.40: 6.40 As the master. God does not avenge his own injuries, but by bearing wished to make persecutors milder; the disciples, who are men, ought to imitate this rule of perfection.
6.41: 6.41 And why see you, etc. One truly sinning cannot chastise the sinner, because those who, prevented by pride, or hatred, or other vice, judging these light or nothing, sharply rebuke those whom they see disturbed from a state of mind, by anger or some light sin, such love rather to vituperate and condemn than to correct and amend. You consider not. The open eye sees badly, boasting namely of itself, while it wishes to heal others, but the blind cannot look at itself while in this it falls worse.
6.42: 6.42 Hypocrite. If you wish to reprove anyone, first see if you are like him. If you are, groan together, and do not wish him to obey you, but exhort him to strive together. But if you are not like, yet because you once were or could be, condescend, and rebuke not from hatred but mercy. Rarely therefore, and not without great necessity, are rebukes to be applied, and only with regard to God, the beam removed from the eye. For these out of hatred or spite undertake to accuse everything and wish to seem counselors, without example of their own amendment. But first they ought to take the beam of envy or malice or simulation out of the secret of their heart, that they may be able to cast out the mote of anger or some spite from the eye of their brother.
6.43: 6.43 There is no tree, etc. A tree good or bad, not by nature, which by God is created good in all, but good or bad will. Fruit, works, which neither can be good of a bad will, nor bad of a good. Neither a tree. If you wish to have true justice and not feigned, what you show by words fulfill by deeds, that you may be a good tree and adorned with good fruits. For though the hypocrite feign, he is not good who does evil works, and if he reprehends the innocent, he is not therefore bad who does good works. And note that here the discourse is of manifest things.
6.44: 6.44 For every tree. The wicked are known by their fruit, while they oppress the good, and blaspheme God if not in words yet in deeds: and chiefly by impatience they are known in the time of adversity. For fasts and prayer and the like are of the simulated as of the good: but the sheep ought not to lay aside their skins, even if sometimes wolves cover themselves with them. It is known. Not by the garment, but by the works that are done by them, they are known. Because as a thorn does not make a grape, so a good tree makes good, a bad bad, and not the converse. For neither of thorns. Not of thorns, that is the cares of the world, figs, that is the sweetness of the resurrection, nor of a bramble, that is the pricking of vices, a grape, that is the fruit of the soul. Which like a grape near the earthly is corrupted, in the higher ripened. Or from the flesh which begets thorns and thistles we do not gather Christ, who hung on the tree like a grape. The thorn and bramble, the heretics, from whom no wise man will be able to find holiness or virtue, but they tear and bloody those approaching. Or thorns and brambles, the cares of the age and pricks of vices. The grape and fig, the sweetness of the new conversation which Christ hungers for in us, and the fervor of love which gladdens the heart of man. Not of thorns and brambles a grape or fig, because the mind of the old man, still pressed by custom, can indeed simulate but not bear the fruit of the new man. And if sometimes the deeds or sayings of the wicked profit the good, it is not the wicked who do this, but it is done of them by the counsel of God.
6.45: 6.45 Brings forth good. Loves the enemy. Gives to everyone that asks, and the like. Brings forth evil, etc. Hates a friend, takes away others', gives not his own, and the like, which God judges according to the intention of the heart. And truly, because from a good or bad heart proceeds, the fruit ought to be judged good or bad, because out of the abundance of the heart what lies hid within the mouth speaks, that is the effect proceeds outwardly, both in words and in deeds. This is as to the divine examination to which the mouth of the heart speaks, because from what intention the words proceed he is not ignorant. Because even words which outwardly seem good, because they proceed from a bad root, he judges not good; hence he adds: And why call you me Lord? As if to say: Why do you boast to sprout the leaves of right confession, who show no fruits of good work? From the abundance. By the speech of the mouth, all that is brought forth from the heart in act or thought the Lord signifies. For word is also wont to be put for deed; hence: There was no word that he showed them not, Isaiah 39.
6.46: 6.46 And why, etc. This calling seems the fruit of a good tree, but because it does not proceed from the fatness of charity, God does not judge it good. What, however, the true discernment of good or bad fruits is, he subjoins under another figure:
6.47: 6.47 Every one that comes, etc. After having long disputed of the openly evil, of the truly and simulatedly good, he likens good hearers of the word to himself, the bad to the devil. Because as Christ builds, instructs, governs one Church of various persons of men, to lead them to eternal life; so the good hearer builds himself a heavenly dwelling in the future, to rejoice with Christ at the dedication, by various virtues. And as the devil draws those obeying him from heaven to earthly things and to sins, where there is no foundation, because evil is without substance, and always hurls to worse: so the bad hearer, whether initiated in the mysteries of Christ or wholly alien, as if hurled into a bottomless pit, finds nowhere to hold himself, but when he is come into the depth of evils, he contemns.
6.48: 6.48 He dug deep. He digs deep who by the precepts of humility roots out all earthly things from the hearts of his own from the foundation, that he may not serve God for anything fleeting, that he may have in them an unshaken dwelling. He laid the foundation. Foundations in the plural, the teachers; in the singular, foundation, the teacher of teachers Christ. Morally. The foundations of the house, intentions of good conversation, which through Christian humility, the rubbish of superfluous thoughts being cleared, the perfect hearer plants in himself, doing in himself spiritually what Christ does in the whole Church generally. The flood. This flood elsewhere he calls the gates of hell. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, Matthew 16. This flood happens in three ways, because each is tempted by his own concupiscence, or the wickedness of false brethren, or the open assault of externals. Dashed against. By the force of the river the crisis of the last judgment can be understood, when both Churches are consummated. Every one that exalts himself shall be humbled, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted, Luke 14. That house. Each of our houses is daily beaten either by unclean spirits, or wicked men, or the restlessness of one's own mind, or flesh. And in so far as they trust in their own strength they are bent: in so far as they cling to the unconquerable rock, they cannot be shaken.
6.49: 6.49 Upon the earth, etc. The devil builds the world which is set in the wicked one upon the earth, because he draws to the love of earthly things. He builds without foundation, because sin does not subsist in its own nature, because evil is not a substance, which yet wherever it is done grows together in a good nature or without foundation, that is without bottom. As therefore he who is sunk in a pit is held at the bottom of the pit, so the fallen soul stands as in a certain place of bottom, if it holds itself in some measure of sin. But with the sin into which it falls it cannot be content, while it is daily led to worse, as in the pit into which it fell it finds no bottom to be fixed. And it fell and the ruin, etc. Every conscience that does not abide fixed in hope on God cannot persist in temptations, and is driven the more the more in those things which are of the world it is separated from the higher. And truly all the wicked or feignedly good, any temptation coming on, become worse.
7.1: 7.1 And when he had finished. Beautifully, where he fulfilled the precepts, he teaches the form of carrying out his precepts. For at once the servant of the Gentile centurion is offered to the Lord to be healed, in whom the Gentiles, who were held sick by worldly servitude, are expressed as to be saved by the benefit of God. He entered Capernaum. Of the centurion, etc. He did not enter before he had finished the words, though he did not enter immediately after these words. For before he entered, in that very interval the leper was cleansed, as Matthew puts it.
7.3: 7.3 He sent to him the elders, etc. By divine providence the elders of the Jews are sent, and in their presence the sick man is healed, that they may be inexcusable if they refuse to believe. The centurion sends friends, lest by his presence he seem to burden the modesty of the Lord, and to have provoked duty by duty. It signifies, however, that we who believe from the Gentiles to the Lord cannot ourselves come to him whom we cannot see in the flesh, but to him sitting at the right hand of the Father. The Gentile people like a centurion is attended by a soldiery of virtues and the perfection of spiritual things, which is signified by a hundred. Lofty, seeking nothing earthly from the Lord for himself and his own, but only the joys of eternal salvation: and they supplicate the Lord for the servants, that is for those who are still pressed in fear by the spirit of servitude, that to them gradually advanced to higher things perfect love may cast out fear, 1 John 4. Matthew says the centurion approached, which is to be understood through faith. For through faith one truly approaches God, which is commended in the centurion by the Lord: I have not found so great faith in Israel. Further Luke follows the order in which it was done, that we might be forced to understand how Matthew says he approached.
7.5: 7.5 Our nation. Mystically. The Gentile people (whose figure the centurion bears) is not far from the house of Jesus, though it dares not invite him under its roof, because his salvation is near to them that fear him. He who rightly uses the natural law, that he works the goods he knows, by that approaches him who is truly good. But to those whom the crimes of Gentile error had bound, what is said elsewhere may be applied: For some of them came from afar, Mark 8.
7.6: 7.6 And Jesus went. About to heal powerfully by a word alone, to commend humility he deigns to visit the sick; and he who would not go to heal the ruler's son, lest he seem to have honored riches, goes to the servant, lest he be thought to have spurned the servile condition. Faith shines in works while he heals, but humility works more in affections while he goes. I am not worthy. Because of the conscience of a Gentile life, he thought himself burdened more by the Lord's condescension than helped, and that he could not have Christ as guest, though endowed with faith, yet not yet imbued with the sacraments. But because what human weakness does not presume, divine grace knows how to give, in the figure of the Gentile people, both his faith, not yet catechized, was praised by the Lord and his servant deserved to be healed.
7.8: 7.8 For I also, etc. If I, a man under another, can command lesser ones, how much more you, who have angels serving above all, can through their ministries without bodily presence say to the sickness to depart, and it will depart, and to health to come, and it will come.
7.9: 7.9 Not even in Israel. The faith of this man is preferred even to the more elect and those who see God. Even in this one the faith of the Gentiles is preferred to Israel.
7.10: 7.10 And they that were sent returned. Matthew explains more plainly that, the Lord saying: As you have believed, so be it done to you, the boy was healed, Matthew 8. But it is the custom of blessed Luke to abridge things plainly set forth by others, or even to pass over on purpose what others said briefly, or omitted, to clarify more skillfully. They found the servant. The Lord believing, the servant is healed, because the merit of the Lord can avail even for servants, not only by merit of faith but also by zeal of discipline.
7.11: 7.11 And it came to pass, etc. After healing the sick he raises the dead, because infirmity precedes death. Which is called Nain. Nain is a city of Galilee at the second milestone from Tabor toward the south near Endor, which is a large village. Nain, however, is interpreted wave or commotion.
7.12: 7.12 Now when he came near, etc. BEDE. When the Word made flesh, the Gentile people through the gates of faith, etc., down to which both meanwhile in few of the Jews converted, and at length in the fullness he commands. Behold a dead man was carried out, etc. The dead, who is carried out before many beyond the gate, signifies one sinning criminally, and not covering the sin in the chamber of the heart, but by indication of work or speech as it were through the doors of his city making it known to others. Whom as an only son the mother Church bewails, who though collected from many persons is yet one virgin mother Church, the individuals however sons. The gate by which he is carried out is some of the senses by which one falls into sin. As he who sees to covet, he who hears idle or foul things, he who lends his tongue to quarrels. The only son of his mother. AMBROSE. Adam from the earth is carried by the four elements, whence man consists. The bier is touched, etc., down to when he thinks of avarice, or when for excessive fever he cannot be touched.
7.13: 7.13 And a crowd. Many with the Lord, many with the widow, that the miracle being seen many may become praisers and witnesses of God.
7.15: 7.15 And he sat up. Three dead the Lord raised: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house, that is in thought; the only son of the mother in the gate, that is in word; Lazarus in the tomb, that is in deed.
7.16: 7.16 He has visited. While he both once appointed the Word to be incarnate, and daily sends the Holy Spirit into the hearts of men, that they may be raised.
7.18: 7.18 And told. AMBROSE. Not with simple heart, but envy stimulating, etc., down to and corrected believe in Jesus and, the master asking, say to him: You are he that is to come. BEDE, GREGORY. He does not say, who have come, etc., down to because a fall of love does not hinder faith, for such a fall is religious.
7.22: 7.22 And answering he said to them: Go and tell John what you have seen, etc. Jesus knowing that no one can fully believe without the Gospel, because as faith begins from the Old Testament so it is fulfilled in the New. Asked about himself, he signified he was it not by any word but by deeds, not answering what was asked but the scandal of the messengers.
7.23: 7.23 Blessed. As if to say: Wonderful things indeed I do, but I do not disdain to suffer abject things, and men must beware lest they despise death in me who venerate signs. Who shall not. GREGORY. Who shall not doubt of the power of the divinity. This is not against John, whom he soon so commends, but recalls the unbelieving from perfidy, and explains to John what he asked, because God is the God of saving, and the issues of death belong to the Lord, Psalm 67. After so many signs and virtues seen, the faithful could not doubt of his death, but wonder, but the mind of unbelievers took scandal in him, when even after miracles it saw him dying.
7.24: 7.24 What. Having admonished the disciples of John that they must believe in the Lord's cross, turning to the crowds, he provokes the poor to virtue, lest, lifted up in heart, unstable in mind, weak in counsel, they prefer showy perishables to useful eternals, but rather take up the cross than the trappings of the world. And therefore he praises the person of John, who, having put aside the love of life, did not change even for fear of death the form of justice. The world is compared to a desert, because it is yet uncultivated and barren, into which we are not so to go out as to think that men puffed up in carnal mind and void of virtue and boasting of the glory of the frail world are to be imitated. A reed with the wind. BEDE. By the reed the carnal mind is signified, which, when touched by favor or detraction, bends to either side. But John is not a reed shaken by the wind, because neither did grace make him soft nor anyone's anger harsh, neither prosperity lifted him nor adversity bent him.
7.25: 7.25 Clothed in soft garments. By the garment the human body is understood. By the prophetic example therefore he exhorts to the virtue of undergoing virtue. Behold they that are in costly apparel. By whom, with riches, the limbs are loosed, strangers to the heavenly kingdom, under the right of demons (who are the kings of darkness) they grow old within the dwellings of this world.
7.26: 7.26 More than a prophet. Because an angel: not by nature but by office, who is sent to announce the supreme judge.
7.28: 7.28 But I say. In this he is not preferred to the patriarchs and all men, but is shown equal to the other saints. But he that. Every saint who is already with God is greater than he who is still in the world. Or, I whom the opinion of many makes less am preferred to him in the Church of the saints. Or the last angel of heaven is better than any man.
7.29: 7.29 And all the people. If this is understood as said by the Lord: hearing John, the people is understood to be designated. If it is said as interposed by the evangelist: hearing the Lord himself disputing of John's greatness, it remains to be understood.
7.31: 7.31 To what then, etc. John being praised, he passes to rebuke those who were not moved even by John's preaching, or despise the preaching of Christ himself.
7.32: 7.32 They are like children. The children are teachers humble in spirit. The market place, the synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, in which the rights of the commands of God were established, because they were wont to reproach their fellow citizens that neither, enticed by psalms, they rose to the praises of God with devout heart, by agility of members (which the dancing notes) nor by the dirges (that is the lamentations of the prophets for destructions already made or to be made) were they converted to penance.
7.34: 7.34 The Son of man is come eating and drinking. He came as then so now, you reject both ways of salvation. We lamented to John, we sang to Christ.
7.35: 7.35 Wisdom is justified. He shows that the children of wisdom understand that justice is neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity of bearing want and temperance, not corrupting oneself by abundance. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, Romans 14. Of which not the use but the concupiscence is blamed. Justified, etc. Whatever you think of me, I am nevertheless understood by the apostles to do justly, being the power of God and the wisdom of God, to whom the Father revealed what he hid from the prudent.
7.36: 7.36 He asked. As he had proposed in words, so by deeds he also establishes that wisdom is justified by all her children, because also by Mary penitent after guilt.
7.37: 7.37 In the house. In whose inner house soever you have known wisdom and justice reclining, run to the feet, that is, to the extreme part of wisdom, inquire with tears, confess sins, spread out your hair, that is, lay before him all the dignities of your body, kiss, that is, speak nothing but wisdom. She brought. As many delights as she had in herself, so many holocausts she found of herself. JEROME. The alabaster of ointment, that is, the body with faith, etc., down to that is, the sins of the Jews.
7.38: 7.38 She began to wash. Mary, sister of Lazarus, performed the same office twice: once in Galilee when she first approached with humility and tears, where she received remission of sins. Secondly, in Bethany, no longer named a sinner, but chaste, and therefore devout: there she anoints the feet, here the head.
7.43: 7.43 He to whom he forgave most. According to men, perhaps he offends more to whom he owed more. But by the Lord's mercy the cause is changed, that he who owed more may love more, yet obtain grace. You have judged rightly. The Pharisee is convicted by his own sentence, because like a frenzied man he carries the rope by which he is bound.
7.44: 7.44 I entered into your house. I entered, flesh assumed, into the people of the Jews.
7.46: 7.46 My head with oil you did not anoint. And though that people confessed they believed in God and not in man, yet the very power of the divinity which appeared by miracles they neglected to proclaim with worthy praise. But the Gentile world, while it believes the mystery of the incarnation, proclaims even his weak things with highest praise.
7.47: 7.47 Her sins are forgiven. In the house of the Pharisee, that is in the custody of the law and prophets, not the unbelieving Pharisee but the penitent sinner is glorified, because the ardor of charity in her burned up the rust of offenses.
7.49: 7.49 And they began, who sat together. The sick one healed, they fall sick over her salvation to others.
7.50: 7.50 Your faith has made you safe. Faith saved, because what she asked she doubted not to be able to receive, because she had already received hope from him from whom she sought salvation.
8.1: 8.1 And it came to pass. After the manner of an eagle provoking her young to fly, the Lord little by little clothes his disciples in the nest of faith with the feathers of virtues, by which afterward they may fly higher and instruct others. First he teaches in synagogues, works miracles, spreads fame everywhere, receives crowds, heals, instructs, here he makes disciples, of whom he chose twelve, whom first he teaches in the presence of the crowd, and bestows the usual benefits on the wretched, but now keeps only them with him, that they may hear him more familiarly, to them alone he expounds the more hidden mysteries, and so at last, they being strengthened by the display of his powers as by the protection of wings, he gives them power of healing, and sends them to preach the kingdom of God.
8.2: 8.2 Mary who is called Magdalene. Since Mary traveled with the Lord, and is remembered as ministering to him, he calls her by the famous name Magdalene: where he describes the same as a sinner, reverently he calls her by the general name woman, lest the name of so great fame which we venerate today be darkened by the mark of former error. Mary, bitter sea, on account of the inborn roar of penance with which she, or we, bewail single evils. Seven devils. The same Church of the Gentiles cleansed from the filth of vices, which Mary signifies, Joanna also signifies, once given to the worship of idols, but now redeemed by the piety of Christ, and filled with grace, who was before as it were the wife of the devil.
8.3: 8.3 And Joanna, etc. Joanna, the Lord is her grace, or the Lord is merciful, whose is all we live. The steward of Herod. Whenever any malignant spirit labors for the kingdom of the devil to deceive, he stands as steward of the most impious Herod. Of their substance, etc. It was an ancient custom of the Jews, and was not reckoned a fault, that women should feed and clothe teachers from their substance. Because this among the Gentiles could cause scandal, Paul recalls that he abstained. They ministered therefore carnal things to the Lord whose spiritual things they reaped, to give a form to preachers that they ought to be content with food and clothing, receiving from the people.
8.4: 8.4 And when a great multitude, etc. As often as the word crowd is inserted in the Gospel, as the diversity of men so also the diversity of wills is intimated. For not all followed Christ with the same will but for diverse causes: some for good, some for evil, yet to all the Lord bestows benefits, by teaching, feeding, healing. The sower went out, etc. The Son of God went out from the bosom of the Father, where for creatures there was no access, to sow his seed, he came into the world to bear witness to the truth. Hence, according to the other evangelists, about to speak this parable he is recorded to have gone out of the house, come to the sea, boarded a ship, signifying this same by the position of the body and the progress of the discourse.
8.5: 8.5 By the wayside. The way is the heart worn and dried by the diligent passing of evil thoughts, so that it cannot receive or sprout the seed of the word, but is trodden by the worst thoughts and snatched by demons. Who are therefore called birds of the air, because they are of heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they run about through the air.
8.6: 8.6 Upon a rock. The rock is the untamed heart not penetrated by the plowshare of true faith, in which is no true love and virtue of perseverance.
8.8: 8.8 A hundredfold, etc. Since ten is wont to be taken for perfection (because in the ten precepts of the law the keeping is contained), a hundred, which arises from ten multiplied, is put for great perfection: the heart therefore yields a hundredfold fruit which through love of neighbor obtains the active life, and through love of God the contemplative, and is adorned with the perfection of spiritual virtues.
8.9: 8.9 This parable. Note that this is the first parable that is placed with its interpretation. And one must beware wherever the Lord, asked by the disciples, expounds his words inwardly, lest we wish to understand either otherwise or more or less than he has expounded. He deigned to show this parable himself, that it might be known he spoke figuratively, and teach that the significations of things are to be sought even in those he did not wish to expound.
8.10: 8.10 Seeing. The teachers of the Jews, who by the merit of their perversity are blinded, falsely think themselves seeing.
8.12: 8.12 And they by the wayside. They are sown by the wayside who, with no faith, no understanding, not even with any tempting occasion of usefulness, deign to receive. Further they upon the rock and among thorns are sown, who hear indeed and approve the usefulness of the word and taste the desire, but lest they reach what they long for, are delayed either by terrifying adversities or by flattering prosperities. By these three kinds are designated whoever do not do the word they hear.
8.13: 8.13 For a while they believe. Many hearing a disputation against avarice or luxury, say that the contemners of the world and chaste men are blessed: but when attractive things are presented to their sight, they soon depart from whatever they had rightly thought.
8.14: 8.14 They are choked. Because pleasures and riches by their importunate thoughts as it were strangle with vital breath the throat of the mind, that the good desire cannot enter the heart.
8.15: 8.15 Into the good ground, etc. Into good hearers who strive to hear the word, and lay it up in the belly of memory, and so in due time bring forth the fruit of work, patient amid the prosperous and adverse things of the world. And the good ground with patience yields fruit, because it does good and bears the evils of neighbors with equanimity, and while they humbly look up to the scourges, after the scourges they are received into rest.
8.16: 8.16 No man. These words are put according to the likeness of human custom.
8.17: 8.17 For there is not, etc. As if to say. Let not the fear of the carnal delay you, nor the bad opinion that is now held of you among the unbelieving, for though you appear cheap, your brightness will appear when the Lord shall enlighten the hidden things of darkness, then you also will be crowned, and your adversaries punished.
8.18: 8.18 For whosoever has, etc. These seem said specially to the apostles, to whom out of charity it is given to know the mysteries, and to the perfidious Jews (who through parables hear what they do not understand). It can also be taken generally, because even the clever, by neglecting, deprive themselves of true wisdom and the simple student by labor tastes. For he who has the love of the word, to him will also be given a sense of understanding what he loves. But he who has not the love of hearing, even if by natural wit or studious labor he thinks he understands, will yet taste no sweetness of true knowledge. And whosoever has not. Therefore the slothful sometimes receives wit, that he may be more justly punished for negligence, who scorned to know what he could have attained without labor, and sometimes the studious is oppressed by slowness of understanding, that he may find greater rewards the more studiously he labors.
8.24: 8.24 And it ceased, and there was a calm. Note that every creature feels the Creator. He commands, rebukes, they feel the commander, not that, according to the heresy of some, they are living beings, but they are sensible to the majesty of the Maker, which are insensible to us.
8.25: 8.25 They wondered one to another. Not the disciples but the sailors and others who were in the ship wonder. Hence Matthew: But the men wondered, saying: What manner of man is this? Matthew 8. But if we say the disciples wondered, they too are rightly called men. To the country of the Gerasenes. Gerasa a city of Arabia by Mount Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh, not far from the lake of Tiberias, signifies the Gentiles whom after the passion and resurrection the Lord visited through preachers, hence Gerasa or Gergesenes casting out the inhabitant, that is the devil by whom it was before inhabited or as a stranger approaching, who was far off in time.
8.27: 8.27 In the tombs. What else are the bodies of the perfidious but certain sepulchres of the dead, in which the words of God do not dwell?
8.28: 8.28 Jesus Son of God. Arius contends he is a creature whom the demon confesses to be the Son of God. The Jews say: He casts out demons by the prince of demons, whom the demons deny to have anything in common with them. It is the devil's torment to cease from harming man, and the longer he had possessed, the harder he lets go. Let anyone therefore who is harmed by the devil beware, that he break his yoke quickly, because the more easily the sooner his dominion is avoided.
8.29: 8.29 He was bound with chains. The chains and fetters are the hard and heavy laws of the Gentiles, by which also in their commonwealth sins were restrained. Yet these laws being broken, they were led by cupidity to those crimes which exceeded common custom.
8.30: 8.30 Because many devils were entered, etc. Many demons which oppress one signify many forms of idolatry worship in one people of the Gentiles. On the contrary it is said: The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, Acts 4. Hence well in Babylon the unity of tongues was split, in Jerusalem it was united.
8.31: 8.31 And they besought. The demons knew that by the coming of the Lord they would one day be plunged into the abyss: not foreknowing the future themselves, but recalling what the prophets said of them.
8.32: 8.32 A herd of swine. The swine are men devoid of voice and reason, given to filthy acts, feeding on the mountain of pride. And unless one live after the manner of a swine, the devil does not receive power in him, or receives it only to try, not to destroy.
8.34: 8.34 They fled and told it in the city and in the villages. The herdsmen fled, because neither the philosophers of the Gentiles nor the princes of the Synagogue can give medicine to the perishing, and though they flee the Christian law yet they proclaim its power by astonishment and wonder.
8.35: 8.35 And they went out to see what was done, and came to Jesus, and found the man, etc. It signifies the multitude delighted by their pleasant life, honoring indeed but unwilling to suffer the Christian religion, while they say they cannot fulfill it. They wonder also at the faithful people healed from former conversation, and sitting at the feet of the Lord, that is, with sound examination of mind beholding the footsteps of the Savior to follow, and clothed with the pursuits of virtues, which deceived he had lost.
8.37: 8.37 And they besought. Conscious of frailty, they judge themselves unworthy of the Lord's presence, not taking in the word of God, and in a weak mind not bearing the weight of wisdom, and therefore he was not troublesome longer, but returns because he deigns not to heal the unwilling, but quickly leaves the weak, to whom he sees his presence a burden.
8.39: 8.39 Return to your house, etc. Allegorically. After the remission of sins one must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel, for the salvation of others also, that then he may rest with Christ, lest when he already wishes to be near with Christ he neglect the mystery of preaching fitted for fraternal deliverance, hence the Apostle: I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, Philippians 1., a thing by far the better, but to abide in the flesh is needful for you.
8.43: 8.43 On physicians. The physicians, the demons, who as though counseling men demand to be worshiped for God, whom the Gentile world had served.
8.44: 8.44 She touched the hem. He touches the hem who loves and believes perfectly the mysteries of the Incarnation, until he arrive at taking greater things. If we consider how great our faith is, and understand how great the Son of God is, we see that in comparison with him we touch only the hem, we cannot reach the upper part of his garment. And immediately, etc. About to raise the dead girl, he returned to make faith, first he cures the woman with the issue. So Elizabeth barren is shown about to bear that the virgin about to conceive may be believed.
8.45: 8.45 Who is. He does not ask to be taught what he knows not but that the faith of the woman may appear.
8.46: 8.46 For I also know. Whoever touches does not lie hid: God needs no eyes to see, nor does he perceive bodily, but has in himself the knowledge of all. Even the power which is propitious to all our iniquities and heals all our infirmities goes out not from us but from God.
8.47: 8.47 And the woman seeing. This modest woman touches the hem, faithful she approached, religious she believed: wise she knows she is healed: so the people of the Gentiles who believed God blushed at sin to forsake it, brought faith to believe, showed devotion to ask, put on wisdom to feel her health herself, took confidence to confess that she was snatching what was another's.
8.51: 8.51 The father of the maid. The father of the maid, the company of the teachers of the law, the scribes and Pharisees, who if they will believe, even the subject Synagogue will be saved.
8.52: 8.52 And they wept. They weep who see the Synagogue estranged from God, who is life, and grieve, and think she can no more be quickened, and she who lost the presence of the bridegroom by which she ought to live lies as dead among the mourners, nor understands even this, why she is mourned. Weep not. Let them weep their dead who think them dead, where there is faith of resurrection there is no death but hope of rest. She is not dead, etc. The maid is dead to men who cannot raise: not to God, to whom the soul lives, and the flesh in being raised sleeps.
8.53: 8.53 They laughed him to scorn, etc. Rightly are they shut out who preferred to deride than to believe, unworthy to see the miracle of the resurrection.
8.54: 8.54 Taking her by the hand. He takes the hand, because unless the hands of the Jews (which are full of blood) are first cleansed, the Synagogue will not rise. Maid, arise. Whoever from the death of the soul, Christ strengthening his hand, comes to himself, ought to rise from the filth of vices, and (as Mark says) to walk in good works, and it is necessary that he soon be fed with heavenly bread, that is the word of God and of the altar.
8.56: 8.56 Whom he charged. As a public harm needs a public remedy, so light sins and secret ones can be blotted out by lighter penance. Hence the girl lying in the house rises with few witnesses, and the same are forbidden to publish the miracle.
9.1: 9.1 And Jesus calling together. The power of signs being first granted, they are sent to preach the kingdom of God, that the greatness of the promises be attested also by the greatness of deeds, and the power shown might give faith to the words, and those who preached new things might do new things.
9.3: 9.3 Take nothing. In Mark it is read, that they should take nothing for the way but a staff only, Mark 6. But it is to be known that both were commanded by the Lord, that they bear nothing but a staff, and that they bear not even a staff. Not to bear a staff is not to be solicitous for what is necessary to human sustenance, because these are due to preachers from those to whom they preach, when they can be received without scandal. To bear nothing but a staff is to use that power of receiving necessaries which is given to preachers. Two coats. A simple garment is whatever is necessary to anyone according to the quality of place or time. A double is what is beyond necessity. Allegorically, in two coats he forbids duplicity.
9.4: 9.4 There abide. Do not run about through houses and change the rights of inviolable hospitality. Hence according to Matthew the house in which they ought to abide is first to be chosen, that the necessity of changing lodging may be removed.
9.5: 9.5 The dust of your feet. The dust is shaken off for a testimony of their labor that they entered the city, and the preaching reached them. Or, it is shaken off that they receive nothing from those who spurned the Gospel, not even the necessaries of life.
9.8: 9.8 John is risen. Those who said John, of whom they had seen no sign, had risen, through the highest malice denied that Jesus had risen, they had seen many wonderful works, in whose passion many wonders had happened.
9.10: 9.10 They told. The apostles tell the Lord what they had done, and how they had taught, how John suffered while they taught. Hence follows: And taking. Not to the idle, not in the city of the Synagogue, that is to those sitting in secular dignity, but among the deserts to those seeking Christ the nourishment of heavenly grace is imparted. For those who are not fastidious are received by Christ, and spiritually and bodily, even if in need they are cured. And note that after the mention of John's passion is complete, Christ feeds, because after the failure of the law the evangelical food begins. Finally after the woman was healed who bears the figure of the Church, and after the apostles were sent to preach, mention is made of the refreshment, because through the apostles in the Church true refreshment is made.
9.11: 9.11 They followed him. Not on beasts, not in vehicles, but by the labor of their own feet, to show the ardor of their mind. He healed. No one receives the food of Christ unless he has first been healed, because after the remission of sins heavenly nourishment is given.
9.12: 9.12 Now the day began. The day declined he feeds, because either the end of the ages drawing near, or when the sun of justice set, we were saved from spiritual hunger. And note the order of the mystery: first by remission of sins medicine is given to the wounds, afterward the nourishment of the heavenly table is spent.
9.13: 9.13 Unless perhaps. The apostles had not yet understood that the faith of the believing people is not for sale, but they knew we are rather to be redeemed through his free foods.
9.14: 9.14 Five thousand. By five thousand are signified those who in secular habit still, through the five senses of the body, know how to use well the outward things they possess. Who are fed with five loaves, because such must yet be instructed by legal precepts and restrained by legal fear. For those who wholly renounce the world are four thousand because of the evangelical doctrine, and are refreshed with seven loaves, that is by the grace of the sevenfold spirit.
9.15: 9.15 And make them all sit down. According to another evangelist the five thousand sit down upon the hay, because those who still have bodily senses are delighted with better things. For all flesh is grass. The four thousand recline upon the ground, for it is more to press the earth than to lie on hay.
9.16: 9.16 He distributed to his disciples. He provokes the apostles to the breaking of bread, that they confessing they have not, the greatness of the sign may become better known. He hints that through their doctrine fasting hearts are daily to be fed.
9.17: 9.17 And they were filled. That the people eating are satisfied signifies that hunger is to be driven away forever from the elect, because he who has received the food of Christ will not hunger. That the apostles minister proclaims the future division of the Lord's body and blood. Twelve baskets. Why does more remain over for five thousand, less for four thousand? Because the four thousand were three days with Christ, and therefore received more of the heavenly food.
9.18: 9.18 And it came to pass. After the miracle when the crowds wished to make him king, the crowd being dismissed, he fled and went up into the mountain alone to pray, and before the disciples went up into the little ship, they were with him. But he alone prays to the Father. For saints can be joined to the Lord by faith and love, and behold him more excellent than men, and follow his conversation in the flesh with steps of humility, but the incomprehensible secrets of the paternal position he alone penetrates, and alone knows what to pray for. With the disciples, however, he is not found to have prayed, but alone he entreats, because the counsel of God human hearts do not take in, nor can anyone be partaker of inward things with Christ. Whom do the crowds say that I am? About to test the faith of the disciples, he first inquires the opinion of the crowd, lest the faith of the apostles seem confirmed by common opinion, but by the recognition of the truth. Rightly are those named crowds who bear diverse opinions of the Lord, whose speech and sense is unstable and wandering, from whom distinguishing his own he says. But whom do you say that I am?
9.19: 9.19 John the Baptist. The opinion about John was perhaps because, placed in his mother's womb, he perceived the presence of the Lord. About Elijah, because he was caught up into heaven, and is believed to be coming. About Jeremiah, because he was sanctified in his mother's womb.
9.20: 9.20 But you. He who treats should consider the persons of the hearers, lest he be mocked before he is heard. The Christ of God. He embraced all, who expressed both nature and name. For in the name of Christ is expression of both divinity and incarnation and the faith of the passion. The heretic, though he deny not the name of Christ, yet denies Christ, who confesses not all that are Christ's.
9.21: 9.21 He charged that, etc. He bids the disciples be silent to deceive the prince of the world, and to avoid boasting, to teach humility. At the same time lest the disciples, still unlearned and imperfect, be oppressed by the weight of greater preaching.
9.23: 9.23 And he said. What pertains to the faith of the Lord's nativity or passion he opened apart to the disciples alone, but this to all. Let him deny himself. Unless one fail himself, he does not draw near to him who is above himself: and does not lay hold of the newness to which he is called unless he slay the oldness in which he was born; and when he ceases from vices let him seek also virtues, whence it is added:
9.24: 9.24 For whosoever. GREGORY. As in time of persecution the soul is to be laid down, so in peace earthly desires are to be broken, that the more secure a man seems, the more anxious he be to guard himself.
9.26: 9.26 Him the Son of man. The voice of profession is not enough to prove faith, which the profession of generality defends from shame.
9.27: 9.27 There are some standing here. He who stands with Christ tastes not death, because he will not have even a slight sense of eternal death who has deserved the fellowship of Christ, in whom even in death the order of living is not interrupted. Till they see the kingdom. Because it was hard to offer the soul to dangers, the body to death, he sustains the weakness of the human mind by the reward of present things, lest it be broken by despair or weariness. For the eternal glory being seen, though in passing and for a brief moment, they are yet made stronger against the adversities of the world. He promises therefore the future glory to be seen on earth in passing, that eternal may be more surely hoped in heaven. Or he promises that some of the disciples will see the spread of the Church before they depart the world by death, that in the present, raised up against the glory of the world, they may more surely be believed to reign in heaven.
9.28: 9.28 After these words. Others who number only six days signify that after the six ages of the world the saints are to rest from labor. Luke, who counts both the first on which the promise is made and the last on which the promise is fulfilled, hints that the resurrection is on the eighth. For as Christ after the sixth day of the sabbath on which he ascended the cross, and after the seventh of the sabbath on which he rested in the sepulchre, rose on the eighth day: so we, after the six ages of the world in which we suffer and labor for the Lord, and after the seventh of the rest of souls which meanwhile is passed in the other life, shall rise in the eighth age. He took Peter. He says only three, because many are called, few chosen, Matthew 20., and those who keep the faith of the Trinity inviolate deserve to rejoice in the eternal vision. The knower of merits knew the three apostles were more perfect than the rest. They signify those who have faith, hope, charity. Or by Peter, rulers or married, by James penitents or active, by John, virgins or contemplatives.
9.29: 9.29 And it came to pass. Transfigured, he did not lose the substance of true flesh, but showed the glory, either of his own or of our resurrection, who as then to the apostles so after the judgment will appear to all the elect. For in the judgment itself both to good and bad he will appear in the form of a servant that they may see him whom they pierced. And his raiment. The raiment of the Lord are the saints who have put on Christ. Which raiment, the Lord abiding on earth, seemed contemptible and like others', but the Lord ascending the mountain shines, because it has not yet appeared what we shall be, but at length we shall be like him, when we shall see him as he is. Or the garments of the word are the discourses of the Scriptures, and certain garments of divine understanding. Because as to those apostles he appeared in another form and his raiment shone, so even to the eyes of your mind the sense of divine reading grows white.
9.30: 9.30 Behold two men. It is to be noted that not the bodies or souls of Elijah or Moses appeared, but those bodies were formed from some subject creature: it can also be believed that by angelic ministry that was done, that angels assumed their persons. Dead and living appear, to signify that Christ was about to die and afterward to live, and that we may live to Christ and die to the world. He gives also to the apostles a sign from heaven, that their faith may be increased. But to the scribes tempting he would not give, that they might be hardened. And Moses and Elijah were seen. By Moses, those of hell; by Elijah, the heavenly; by the apostles, the earthly, who are to come to judgment, are signified.
9.31: 9.31 They spoke of his decease. Moses, that is the lawgiver, and Elijah the eminent of the prophets appear with the word, to show that he is the one who spoke in the law and the prophets, and whom the law and the prophets promised. Who were seen not in the low places but on the mountain, because only those lofty in mind discern the majesty of the Scripture which was fulfilled in the Lord.
9.32: 9.32 They were heavy with sleep. They are weighed down with sleep, because by the splendor of incomprehensible deity the sense of the human body is oppressed. Or they are weighed down with sleep, that they might see the glory of the resurrection after the rest of the body, and the saints will see the majesty of the Lord the more truly, the more they rejoice in the immortality of their flesh in which they conquered death. Then they will behold Moses and Elijah in glory, because they will better understand how one jot or one tittle shall not pass from the law, Matthew 5., and how the Lord did not destroy the law and the prophets but fulfill them.
9.33: 9.33 It is good for us to be here. He who had climbed the heights does not wish to descend to earthly things, but always to persevere on high, and Peter is in the person of those entering the kingdom of God. It is good for us to be here. It is good to be in the kingdom of God. As if to say: We alone will enjoy this light, not the envious Jews. Three tabernacles. That is, words, thoughts, works. One for Moses. How do they know those whom they had not seen before? By the majesty coming upon them, as in the future resurrection each will know another, and what is desired in the other the other will understand by charity.
9.34: 9.34 There came a cloud and overshadowed them. Though Peter from weakness knows not, the devotion of obedience pleases. Hence the cloud overshadows, this is the overshadowing of the divine Spirit, which does not darken the affections of men, but reveals hidden things, whose perfect is shown by the voice heard saying: This is my Son. Because he sought a material tabernacle, he received the shelter of a cloud, that he may learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the rule of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit. And they feared. They fear, because human frailty cannot bear the sight of greater glory, and the more anyone seeks higher things the more he falls to lower if he knows not his own measure.
9.36: 9.36 And a voice. The voice of the Father, the terror removed, teaches Peter the truth. And note that, as at the baptism of the Lord, so at his transfiguration the mystery of the Trinity is declared, because the glory which we confess in baptism we shall see in the resurrection. The Spirit in a dove, here in a bright cloud, because he who now keeps the faith with simple heart will then contemplate in open light of vision what he believed, and by the very grace by which he shall be enlightened be protected. Jesus was found alone. Not Elijah, not Moses, but him whom you see alone, to him the tabernacle must be fixed in the heart. They depart therefore where the Lord began to be designated, lest the voice of the Father be thought sent to servants.
9.37: 9.37 And it came to pass the day following, when they came down from the mountain. According to the quality of merits, daily the Lord ascends to some, while he glorifies the perfect, whose conversation is in heaven, by lifting them higher, and instructs and teaches of eternal things which the crowd cannot hear. To others he descends, while he strengthens and teaches and chastises the earthly and beginners. The crowd met them. On the mountain he prays, teaches, shows his majesty, opens the voice of the Father to the apostles, coming down he is received by the crowd, is beset by the weeping of the wretched, reproaches the sins of unbelief, drives out evil spirits.
9.39: 9.39 And behold a spirit seized. Matthew describes a lunatic, Mark a deaf and dumb. It signifies those who, like the moon, change, never remaining in the same state, but through diverse vices wax and wane, who neither confess the faith nor wish to hear the word of the faith itself.
9.42: 9.42 And as he was coming. While the boy comes to the Lord, he is dashed down, because those converted to the Lord are for the most part more gravely beaten by the demon, either to be brought back to vices, or that the devil may avenge himself for his expulsion. As in the beginning of the nascent Church he set many and grave contests against those whom he saw withdrawn from his kingdom.
9.43: 9.43 And he rebuked. Not the boy suffering violence but the devil inflicting violence is rebuked, because he who wishes to heal the sinner ought to rebuke and drive out the vice, but cherish the man by loving until he render him healed to the spiritual fathers of the Church.
9.44: 9.44 Lay up. You who cleave to my discipleship, to whom I have more openly opened my secrets, store in mind the outcome of the precious blood by which the world is to be redeemed, while the rest marvel at such deeds of divine altitude. It will come to pass that he be delivered. Amid the great things of divine power he more often repeats the abjects of human passion, lest coming suddenly it terrify, but being foreseen be borne more lightly.
9.45: 9.45 But they understood not. This ignorance arose not so much from slowness as from love, because, still carnal and ignorant of the mystery of the cross, they could not believe that he whom they knew as God would die, but as they were wont to hear him speaking through figures, so also what he said of his betrayal they thought signified figuratively something else.
9.46: 9.46 And there entered a thought. Because they had seen Peter and James and John led apart into the mountain, and some secret delivered to them. But also Peter had been promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven above, and the Church was to be built upon him, they supposed; or that these three were preferred to the rest, or Peter to all the apostles: or because in the payment of the tribute they had seen Peter made equal to the Lord himself, they thought he was to be preferred to the rest. But it is to be known that this question was raised both before and after the tribute was paid.
9.48: 9.48 Whosoever shall receive this child. Or simply: he teaches that the poor of Christ are to be received for his honor by those who wish to be greater. Or he teaches that they be little children in malice, that they keep the simplicity of childlike innocence, that the form of virtue which the child observes by nature as guide they themselves follow of industry for the name of Christ. Receives me. He who receives an imitator of Christ receives Christ, and who receives the image of God receives God.
9.49: 9.49 John said. John, loving God and loved by the Lord, thinks he who does not use obedience is to be excluded from the benefit, therefore he is taught that no one is to be kept from the good which he has in part, but rather to be provoked to what he has not yet. Such also are judged to be admitted for the salvation of others. In heretics therefore or bad Catholics, we ought to detest and forbid not the common sacraments in which they are with us and are not against us, but the division contrary to peace and truth by which they are against us and follow not the Lord with us.
9.50: 9.50 Forbid not. For he that. John is not rebuked because he did it out of love, but is taught to know the distance of the weak and the strong, because the Lord, though he rewards the stronger, does not exclude the weak.
9.54: 9.54 Lord, will you. BEDE. The apostles still rude and ignorant of the manner of avenging, etc., down to such power was conferred on holy men by God. We say that fire come down from heaven. At the word of these fire would come down from heaven, because they are sons of thunder. And consume them? And turning he rebuked them and said. In the likeness of Elijah, who with his own hand and fire divinely obtained put to death the priests of Baal. And in that the apostles presume to themselves the power of such a prophet, there is shown in them the merit of the prophets. AMBROSE. The apostles who follow the law do not sin, etc., down to he does not seek vengeance who does not fear.
9.55: 9.55 You know not of what spirit you are. By whose spirit you are signed, whose acts you imitate, now piously counseling, but in the future justly judging.
9.56: 9.56 The Son of man came not to destroy souls but to save, etc. Perfect virtue has no zeal for revenge, nor is there any anger where is the fullness of charity. BEDE. Not always are those who sin to be avenged, etc., down to by whom in this place fire is kept off.
9.57: 9.57 A certain man said. THE SAME. This man moved by the greatness of the signs wishes to follow, etc., down to and feigned the obedience of a disciple, which feigning is figured by the fox.
9.58: 9.58 Foxes have holes. THE SAME. The fox is a deceitful animal, intent on snares, practicing plunders of fraud, even among the very lodgings of men dwelling in holes: so the heretic, not having the house of faith, draws others into his fraud and seduces them from the faith.
9.59: 9.59 And he said to another. Note the Lord did not spurn faults but frauds, because he who repudiated the fraudulent chose the innocent, but him whose father he knew dead, that father of whom it is said: Forget your people and your father's house, Psalm 44., etc.
9.60: 9.60 Let the dead. BEDE. Mystically. The son is not called away from the office of the father, etc., down to ought not to bury in himself the perfidies of the devil.
9.61: 9.61 To renounce those. If the disciple about to follow God is rebuked because he wishes to renounce his house, what will become of those who without any usefulness often visit the houses of their own which they have left.
10.1: 10.1 And after these things, etc. BEDE. As in the apostles is the form of bishops, etc., down to as the sun is wont to make a threefold circuit of its light in seventy-two hours. He sent them two and two. By sending them two and two it is hinted that no one ought to undertake the office of preaching who has not charity toward another. Or two and two are sent, according as two and two animals were sent into the ark, that is male and female, unclean first in carnal generation, but cleansed by the sacrament of the Church through spiritual grace in the preaching of the disciples.
10.2: 10.2 The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few. The harvest, the crowd of believers, the laborers the apostles and their followers. And although the harvest is sown by the word of God, yet it requires the labor of cultivation and the anxious duty of the laborer, lest the birds of the air scatter the sown seeds.
10.3: 10.3 As lambs among wolves. As the wolf lies in wait for sheep, so the heretic for the faithful. And as the wolf circles the fold by night, not daring to enter, the dog's sleep exploring the absence or sloth of the shepherd, so the heretic in the night of his interpretation tries to deceive the faithful, not entering the Church, strives to avoid, or kill, or send into exile the pastors of the Church. The wolf is by nature of body rigid, cannot easily bend, so the heretic is not wont to recall the intention of a hard heart from error.
10.4: 10.4 Carry no purse nor scrip. So great ought to be the preacher's trust in God that, though he do not foresee the expenses of the present life, he yet know most certainly they will not fail him, lest while the mind is occupied with temporal things it preach eternal ones less. Salute no man by the way. He commands to hasten and press on, lest by the conversation of anyone they meet they be turned back from the journey enjoined. He does not simply say: Salute no man, since it is the use of humanity to salute others, but added, by the way, because the diligence of salutation is not taken away, but the obstacle of hindering devotion is abolished, that when divine things are commanded human things be for a little set aside.
