10.7: 10.7 And in the same house. If your peace be received, it is fit that you abide in it, receiving carnal stipends from those to whom you offer heavenly things. Behold he who forbade purse and scrip grants expenses from preaching, yet so that they be content with the food and drink offered. Remain. One must not wander from house to house with vagrant facility, that constancy be kept in hospitable love, lest the bond of friendship once formed be easily dissolved. For the laborer is worthy. Note that to the one work of preachers two wages are due: one on the way, which sustains us in labor; another in the fatherland, which rewards us in the resurrection.
10.8: 10.8 And into whatsoever city. Having described the diverse lodging of the house, he teaches what they ought to do also in cities, namely to communicate with the pious in all things, to be separated from the society of the impious in all.
10.11: 10.11 Even the dust. He commands them to shake off the dust: either to attest the earthly labor which they vainly undertook for them; or to show they so seek nothing earthly from them that they will not suffer even the dust of their land to cling to them.
10.12: 10.12 That it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in that day. The Sodomites, though they burned in vices and were inhospitable, yet among them no guests such as the prophets among the Jews, such as the apostles were found. Lot among them, though just, taught nothing, did no signs. And therefore of him to whom much is given, much is required, and the mighty shall mightily suffer torments, Wisdom 6.
10.13: 10.13 Woe to you, Chorazin. Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum and Tiberias are cities of Galilee, on the shore of the lake of Genesareth. These the Lord bewails, because after so many miracles and virtues they did not do penance: and are worse than the Gentiles, who dissipated only the natural law, because after the contempt of the written law they feared not to trample the Son of God too, and ungrateful to spurn grace. And sitting in ashes. We see the words of the Savior fulfilled, because when those aforesaid cities, the Lord present, would not believe, Tyre and Sidon were once friends of David and Solomon, and afterwards, the disciples of Christ evangelizing, devoutly received the faith. Why it was preached to those who would not believe and not preached to those who would believe he knows who knows all things.
10.16: 10.16 He that hears you hears me. In hearing or despising the preacher of the Gospel let everyone know he despises or hears not vile persons but the Savior himself, because in the disciple the master is heard, and in the Son the Father honored.
10.17: 10.17 Lord, even. Well they confess, giving honor to the name of Christ: but because, with faith still weak, they rejoice in virtues and are elated by the working of signs, they are frightened by the example, and recalled to humility. For if the devil was cast headlong from heaven for pride, much more these produced from the earth, if they grow proud, shall be humbled.
10.19: 10.19 Upon serpents and scorpions. The serpents are bad men or demons who cast the poison of wicked persuasion at virtues begun. The scorpions, who strive to spoil virtues about to be consummated at the end.
10.20: 10.20 Rejoice not that the spirits, etc. To cast out evil spirits and work other virtues is sometimes not the merit of him who does them, but the invocation of the name of Christ does this, to the condemnation of those who invoke, or to the profit of those who see and hear: where, though men despise those who work signs, yet they honor God, at whose invocation miracles are done. He forbids rejoicing at the humiliation of the devil, who fell by pride, but let them rejoice in their own exaltation: that whence they fell, lifted up, these may ascend humbled. But rejoice. If anyone shall have done heavenly or earthly works, by these as by letters adorned he is fixed eternally in the memory of God.
10.21: 10.21 In that very hour. When he spoke of the subjection of unclean spirits, of the names written in heaven, he shows through what this so great height was given to men, namely through the humility of the Christian faith. I confess to you, Lord. I give thanks, because to the apostles of my coming you have opened the sacraments, which the scribes and Pharisees, who seem wise to themselves, know not. You have revealed them. He does not say, to the foolish and dull, but to little ones, that is the humble, to prove that he condemned swelling, not sharpness. Yea. He does not give the reason why he chose these and reprobated those, but says so it pleased God. In which we receive an example of humility, lest rashly we examine the heavenly counsels. All things, etc. Humility, by which one comes to faith, being commended, beautifully the passage is connected on faith itself, when he says all things are delivered to him, not the elements which he himself created, but those little ones to whom the Father revealed the mysteries of the Son. When you hear all things, you acknowledge the Omnipotent, not discolored, not degenerate from the Father. When you hear delivered, you confess the Son to whom by nature of one substance all things are rightly proper, not conferred by gift through grace.
10.24: 10.24 That many prophets. The prophets and the just saw the glory of the Lord from afar through a glass and in a riddle; but the apostles having the Lord present and asking from him what they wished were not taught by angels or various forms of visions.
10.25: 10.25 A lawyer stood up. The doctor of the law who without faith lay in the law stands up to stand: he stands while he calls the master, but even standing he tempts God by being silent about what he was.
10.27: 10.27 He answering said. He said what he had read, but did not fulfill what was written, because in his presence he had the Lord whom he ought to love, but him he calls master, not God.
10.29: 10.29 But he willing. The lawyer, that he might be said to have answered wisely, first confesses he knows not the commandment of the law, because refusing to be humbled, and wishing to justify himself, he cannot see the secrets which are revealed to the little ones of Christ; to whom Christ so tempers the answer that every one who does mercy is understood as neighbor, and especially the Son of God himself who has become neighbor to us through humanity is designated. Who is my. No one is nearer to man than God, who knows within and without, and can care for all, but every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor man for neighbor. A certain man, etc. AUGUSTINE. This man is understood to be Adam in the human race, etc., down to he was nearer than the priest or the Levite of the same nation.
10.31: 10.31 And it chanced, etc. The priest proclaims the law of God: the law indeed came down through Moses into the world, and conferred no healing of this kind. The Levite came down, who shows the type of the prophets, but he too heals none, because the law reproves sins, but passed by, because it grants no indulgence.
10.33: 10.33 Moved with compassion. This is not said of the priest and Levite, because the law has no mercy, but judgment and vengeance.
10.34: 10.34 He brought him to an inn. He calls it not a house but an inn, by which name he signifies the miseries and stenches of this life, lest man in this exile rejoice as in his country.
10.37: 10.37 He that showed. Kinship does not make a neighbor, but mercy, which mercy is according to nature. For nothing is so according to nature as to help a partner of nature.
10.38: 10.38 And it came to pass as, etc. Discourse having been held on the love of God and neighbor, the example of both loves is subjoined, not so much in word alone as in the exhibition of work. For by these two sisters two spiritual lives are signified. By Martha, devotion active in works, by which we are joined in charity to our neighbor. By Mary, the religious intention of the mind on the word of God, by which we sigh in the love of God. The active gives bread, either bodily to the hungry or of doctrine to the ignorant, corrects the erring, recalls the proud to humility, dispenses what is expedient to each: the contemplative keeps the charity of God and neighbor, but rests from outward action, clings to the desire of the Creator alone, and, all cares trodden under, burns to see the face of the Creator, and desires to be mingled with the heavenly citizens, who rejoice in eternal incorruption in the sight of the Lord. Into her house. Jesus entering the house, the wicked life, though it once had been, flees, two innocent lives remain, the laborious and the leisured, between them is the fountain of life itself.
10.39: 10.39 Sitting by. The more humbly she sits, the more she falls. Water flows together to the valley from the swellings of the hill. Mary sits, because the contemplative, the tumults of vices appeased, now enjoys the desired rest of mind in Christ. Martha stands, because the active toils and sweats in the contest.
10.40: 10.40 But Martha. Mary was intent how she might be fed by the Lord, Martha was intent how she might feed the Lord: she prepares the banquet for the Lord, in the Lord's banquet the other is already delighted.
10.41: 10.41 And answering. Mary does not answer, but as one at leisure commits her cause to the judge. For if she prepared a speech to answer she would relax the intention of hearing. Martha, Martha. The repetition is a sign of love, or perhaps of an intention to be warned, that she might hear more attentively.
10.42: 10.42 But one thing is needful. One is preferred to many. For not one from many but many from one, and yet many are necessary to those tending to one. Mary has chosen the best. Martha's part is not rebuked, for it too is good, but Mary's part is praised, which is best, why it is best is subjoined.
11.1: 11.1 And it came to pass. After the history of the sisters (which signify two lives) he introduces the Lord as having prayed, and the disciples as taught to pray, because the prayer he taught contains in itself the mystery of both lives, and the perfection of these lives is to be obtained not by our strength but by prayers. When he ceased. Therefore the Savior is often shown praying, to bring the disciples to zeal for prayer. Hence, the prayer ended, he is asked by the disciples, to teach how they ought to pray.
11.5: 11.5 Which of you shall have a friend. After setting before those asking the form of prayer, he enjoins also the urgency and frequency of praying, that prayer be offered not only by days but also by nights, for he who at midnight asks loaves of a friend and persists in the intention of asking, praying is not defrauded.
11.7: 11.7 Trouble me not. He does not take away the hope of obtaining, but kindles more vehemently the desire of praying, the difficulty of obtaining being shown. The door is now. The door which Paul asks to be opened to him to speak the mystery of Christ, and which John saw opened to him, is the understanding of the divine word, which is closed in the time of famine of the word of God, when understanding is not given. And my children, that is, those who dispensing evangelical wisdom as bread preached through the world, are now with the Lord in eternal rest, and yet by praying it comes about that the one praying receives understanding from the Lord himself, even if man fail through whom wisdom is preached. I cannot rise. AMBROSE. No one fears to wake him who sleeps, whom he knows ever prays watching.
11.8: 11.8 Yet because of his importunity, etc. There are many snares, and the sleep of the body is heavy, because if the mind begins to sleep it loses the vigor of its virtue. Rouse therefore your sleep, that you may knock at the door of Christ, that when you have entered the hidden and dark treasures in Christ Jesus may be opened to you.
11.9: 11.9 Ask and it shall be given you. If a friend, a man, rises and gives, compelled not by friendship but weariness, how much more does God, who without weariness gives most largely what is asked. Lest then the mind, turned from the vanity of error, pine longer in spiritual want, let us ask for the feasts of the word, let us seek the friend who gives, let us knock at the door where hidden things are kept. For he gives great hope who in promising does not deceive. For every one that asks receives. Perseverance is needed that we may obtain. But if to the asker it is given, and the seeker finds, and to the one knocking it is opened, then to whom it is not given, and who does not find, and to whom it is not opened, it appears he has not well sought, asked and knocked.
11.11: 11.11 And which of you if he ask his father bread, will he give him a stone? etc. BEDE. Mystically. Bread signifies charity, because of the greater appetite and necessary use, etc., down to stretches himself forth to those that are before.
11.13: 11.13 How much more. An open comparison. For if man a sinner, still burdened with frail flesh, does not refuse to give temporal things to sons asking, much more the heavenly Father bestows on sons endowed with fear and love of him unfailing goods in heaven.
11.14: 11.14 And he was casting out. After the words of preaching which he set before the humble he works miracles also, that those who do not believe the preacher may believe the miracles seen. Matthew says this demoniac was also blind. In which three miracles are done by the Lord: he sees, speaks, is freed from the demon. What was then done carnally in one is done daily in the conversion of the Gentiles, that first, the demon and all the filth of idolatry being expelled, they see the light of faith, then the mouths silent before are loosed for the praise of God.
11.15: 11.15 In Beelzebub. Ninus king, founder of Nineveh, consecrated a statue to Belus his father, and established divine honors to him, whose likeness of image the Chaldeans receiving called Bel. The Palestinians receiving said Baal, the Moabites Beelphegor. The Jews, however, worshipers of one God, because of derision of the Gentiles called him Beelzebub. For Baal is called man, Zebub fly, whence Beelzebub, that is, man of flies, or having flies, because of the filth of blood which was immolated in his temple. The Jews also asserted that in this idol the prince of demons dwells, by whose power they said Jesus cast out demons.
11.18: 11.18 But he, seeing their thoughts. The Lord reserved this as proper to himself, to look into and judge thoughts. It is proper to the Jews to seek signs, hence Paul: The Jews require signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom, 1 Corinthians 1. But he, seeing. He answers not their words but their thoughts: in which he gives a certain sign of his power by which he searches the secrets of hearts. According to the letter it is plain that every kingdom solid and firm if divided by parts is brought to desolation, emptied of inhabitants, and house shall fall upon house, with the inhabitants of one house by the family of another house either oppressed or punished. Whither these things tend spiritually, he expounds when he adds: If Satan also be divided against himself. If I, as you say, cast out demons by the prince of demons, then the kingdom of the devil is divided against itself, and so the power of his malice cannot stand. If, however, a demon cannot expel a demon, you falsely say that I cast out demons by the prince of demons. If he truly can, as you say, look to yourselves, that you may come out of his kingdom which is divided, lest in its ruin you be equally involved. By whom, however, the Lord casts out demons, lest they think him prince of demons, let them attend to what follows.
11.19: 11.19 And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, your children. The children of the Jews he calls the apostles, who among other miracles which they had received from the Lord also drove out demons. This expulsion they ascribed not to the devil but to God, who were conscious they had learned no evil arts from the Lord. Therefore they themselves, choosing the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, in whom there was no artful malice, shall sit on twelve seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Or, children, that is the exorcists of that nation, who by invoking the name of the Lord expelled demons. As if to say: If the expulsion of demons in them is ascribed not to the devil but to God, why has not the same work in me the same cause? Therefore they themselves shall be your judges. Not by power but by comparison, while they assign the expulsion not to the devil but to God. But if. As if to say: A divided kingdom cannot stand, but the kingdom of Satan is divided, as you say, that Satan expels Satan, therefore, etc.
11.20: 11.20 But if by the finger. The Son is called the hand or arm of the Father: the Holy Spirit is called the finger on account of the difference of various gifts, which are given to men through the Holy Spirit, as the fingers are distinct from each other: nor does the inequality of members hurt. For though the arm is greater than the finger, yet the arm with the finger is one body. With this finger the law was written on tables. This finger the magicians confessed in Egypt. Surely is come, etc., the kingdom. That is, the judicial power of God: by which he will separate the good from the evil on the day of judgment. Or, Kingdom, that is, heavenly beatitude. As if to say: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, you know without doubt that entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened to the believing.
11.21: 11.21 When a strong man armed keeps his court. As if to say: If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, as you say, then in something I would consent to the works of the devil, but in no way do I consent with him, but rather I hasten to overcome him and cast him out from my faithful. When the devil, strong. For harming, armed, with many spiritual wickednesses: keeps, in his servitude, his court, that is the world, which is set in the wicked one, in which until the coming of the Son of God the devil ruled without contradiction, and used an ill-pacified government in the hearts of unbelievers.
11.22: 11.22 But if a stronger. He calls himself stronger, who not by agreeing peace and operation, as they calumniated, but by stronger power laid him low, and freed the world from his dominion. The arms of the devil which he took away are the most subtle wiles of spiritual wickedness. The spoils are the souls deceived by him, which Christ the victor distributes, which is a mark of the triumphant, because leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to men, some apostles, others evangelists, Ephesians 4., etc.
11.23: 11.23 He that is not, etc. And truly my works do not agree with the works of Satan, because I myself in nothing agree with him, but we are altogether contrary, because I am humble, kind, willing to save souls: he proud, envious, desires to destroy. I by my preaching gather virtues; he scatters and separates from the unity of the Church. And he that gathers not. This can be understood superfluously of all heretics or schismatics, who are all excluded from the kingdom of God.
11.24: 11.24 When the unclean spirit. Because you withdraw yourselves from my kingdom, ascribing my works to the devil, therefore the devil dwells in you, as in his own kingdom more gravely than in the beginning. Is gone out. The devil went out from the Jews when this people received the law and worship of the one God, and passed to the Gentiles which were dry and barren of the fatness of the Holy Spirit and love of neighbor. In whom now he finds no rest, because now from the hearts of the Gentiles, the faith of Christ being received, he is expelled, when he says: I will return to the Jews whom I left before. And he finds that people swept with brooms, that is by the superfluous observances of the Pharisees and ceremonies of the law, which now avail nothing after the coming of Christ. And that he may possess more firmly he takes the universality of demons. And now the Israelites are worse, blaspheming Christ in their little assemblies, than they were once in Egypt before the law was received, because greater is the unbelief not to receive one who has come than not to believe one who is to come. Seeking rest and finds none. Because he who feeds on wicked thoughts and acts perceives that all his temptations cease in the minds of the faithful. Then he says: I will return into my house whence I came out. I will return to the conscience of that one from which I had been cast out in baptism, and I will subject the former possession to myself with accustomed dominion.
11.25: 11.25 And when he is come he finds it swept with a besom. Because when he seeks again such a reprobate, offenses compelling, he finds the conscience of the sinner cleansed from vices in baptism, but heaped with no good work.
11.26: 11.26 Then he takes seven. The fullness of all vices. Which spirits, namely, are said to be worse than the devil, because though the devil is evil, yet those who are enslaved to vices by their own merits driving them are not only evil but also strive to show the appearance of goodness by affected virtues through hypocrisy. And the last state of that man. It were better to be ignorant of the way of truth than after the knowledge to turn back.
11.27: 11.27 Blessed. Here Mary is praised who bore the Lord. And the depravity of the Jews both present and of the heretics to come who deny the true humanity of Christ is confuted, because she confesses the true Son of God against the blaspheming Jews, and witnesses the true son of man, consubstantial with the mother. For unless he were one flesh with the mother, in vain would that womb of the virgin and breasts be blessed. And the paps. According to the physicians from the same source milk to nourish and seed to procreate children flows, therefore he who could be nourished with her milk could be conceived of the seed of the virgin.
11.28: 11.28 Yea rather. As if to say: Not only Mary is to be praised, because she bore the Word of God in the womb, but chiefly blessed, because she kept the precepts of God in work. So also all are blessed who conceive the word of God by the hearing of faith and bring forth and nourish the keeping of good work in their own heart or their neighbors'. Who hear. In praise of the Church. On the contrary the Pharisees are condemned, who sought neither to hear nor to fulfill the word of God but to blaspheme.
11.29: 11.29 He began to say. Some calumniated his works, to whom thus far he has answered. Others tempting sought a sign from heaven, and to them he here answers. It seeks a sign and a sign shall not be given it, etc. To the disciples he gave a sign of divinity, both first transfigured on the mountain, and afterward lifted up into heaven while they saw. But to the unbelieving from the lower passion of humanity.
11.31: 11.31 The queen of the south shall rise. Here, the people of the Jews being condemned, the mystery of the Church is expressed, which in the Ninevites through penance (which abolishes sin) in the queen of the south the zeal for receiving wisdom (which guards against sin) is gathered from all the ends of the world, to know the words of the true Peacemaker. For the Church consists of two, that you either cease to sin or know not how to sin. In the judgment. Not a thousand years before the judgment as the Jews feign, but in the judgment itself shall she rise. With the men. BEDE. Behold the common resurrection is shown, of the good as of the bad. Shall condemn. Not by power of judgment but by comparison of better act, because, leaving her empire, she came into Judea to hear a man famous for wisdom, but the Jews do not hear the true wisdom of God conversing with them, but blaspheme. In the preaching. Jonah preached a few days, Christ a long time. He to strangers, Christ to his own citizens. He did no sign, Christ did many.
11.33: 11.33 No man. BEDE. He who in the figure of the queen and the Ninevites preferred the Church to the Synagogue, etc., down to they refuse to enter by believing the open door of light.
11.35: 11.35 Take heed therefore lest, etc. After the institution of right faith he instructs also about good works and good intention, that not only works but also thoughts and intentions of the heart be cleansed, as if to say: I kindle the lamp of faith in your senses, and set it in the Church. But you, as much as is in you, kindle your lamps, that is cleanse the intentions of your heart, that from clean intention the works also may please. These said specially against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees craftily seeking signs, according to the moral sense instruct us generally.
11.37: 11.37 And as he was speaking. He does not say, when he spoke these things, but, as he was speaking. In which it is hinted that not immediately on finishing these words but other things interposed he turned aside to the Pharisee, because this discourse finished while he was yet speaking, behold his mother and brethren sought to speak to him. Of whom after he answered the one telling him: He that does the will of my Father, he is my brother and sister and mother, afterwards he went in to the Pharisee's banquet. Why not baptized. The Jews frequently wash their hands before they eat, holding the tradition of the elders, and returning from the market they do not eat unless they be baptized.
11.39: 11.39 Of the cup. Mark relates that the Jews were accustomed to observe baptisms of cups and pitchers and couches and brass vessels. The cup, a glass vessel; the dish, earthen. By this the fragility of the human body is figured, in which outwardly they put forward holiness and feign justice, they washed what was outside, within most wicked. But that which is within is yours. Let no one think fornication and bodily vices of the kind are alone grave, and spiritual vices light, like avarice, anger, pride, etc., as the Pharisees thought.
11.41: 11.41 But yet that which remains. Now the good teacher teaches how the contagion of the body ought to be cleansed. And here is more widely explained what he had said briefly above of cleansing the eye of the heart. For this whole place is directed to this, to invite us to the zeal for simplicity, and condemn the superfluous and earthly things of the Jews, who understanding the law according to the body are compared to glass and dish because of fragility. In which, though they sin gravely, yet absolution of sin is promised them if they strive to do mercy. What remains over necessary food and clothing give to the poor. Or I give counsel, what only remains after so many crimes, give alms. The first alms is to heal your souls by believing in me who cleanse hearts, and, hearts being cleansed by faith, all things even outward will be clean. He who wishes to give alms in order begins from himself, and gives it first to himself. For alms is a work of mercy, hence it is said: Have pity on your own soul pleasing God.
11.42: 11.42 Passing over judgment. Briefly he touched many of their vices, who intent on tithing small things have not the fear of the future judgment and the charity of God. They pass over judgment, because they do not refer all they do to judgment. They pass over charity, because they love God not from affection. But again, lest faith make you studious and negligent of works, he subjoins the perfection of the faithful man, that after faith he work.
11.44: 11.44 Who are as sepulchres. Here he reproves the superstition of the teachers themselves, who outwardly put forward the appearance of right doctrine, but the foulness which they bear within they conceal.
11.45: 11.45 And one answering. The word of God heard, the Pharisee from evil conscience thinks insult is done to him, and the punishment of the perfidious recalled, he understands himself to be condemned.
11.47: 11.47 Woe to you. They are not charged because they adorn the tombs of the prophets, but because they imitate the slayers of the prophets, by building sepulchres they accuse the crimes of the fathers. But by persecuting Christ and the apostles they imitate the crimes of the fathers, and the sentence of damnation which they pronounced on the fathers they turn back on themselves.
11.48: 11.48 Truly. To court the favor of the crowd you build, as if you abhorred their crimes, but by the work itself you show that you consent to their perfidy, because you do not do this good well but for vainglory. But you. Because you are imitators of them, to fulfill what was lacking to the fathers, namely that you persecute me and mine, whom they persecuted in the prophets.
11.49: 11.49 I will send prophets and apostles, and of them they will kill and persecute. The heretics lie who say that one is the founder of the Old, another of the New Testament.
11.50: 11.50 From this generation. All the wicked are one generation, one city, one body of the devil, as all the good are called one generation and one body.
11.51: 11.51 To the blood of Zechariah. Why to him, when after him many were killed before the birth of Christ, and, Christ born, soon boys were slain by this generation? But because Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and killed in the field, Zechariah a priest killed in the court of the temple, they signify two orders of martyrs, laymen, and those who are devoted to the office of the altar.
11.52: 11.52 For you have taken away the key. The key, the humility of Christ, which those who have understand the Scriptures. This the lawyers neither themselves in the law and prophets understand, nor wish to be understood by others. To enter the key is not to be content with the surface of the letter but to penetrate to the understanding of secrets. Or a teacher if he scandalizes by example those whom he builds by word neither himself enters the kingdom of God and shuts out those who could enter.
11.53: 11.53 And as he said these things to them, the Pharisees and lawyers began. How true were the charges of perfidy, feigning and impiety which they heard they themselves testify, who under so great thundering whirlwind do not come to themselves but assail the teacher of truth.
12.1: 12.1 Beware. To this leaven belong all that he disputed above in the house of the Pharisee, hence the Apostle: Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice, 1 Corinthians 5., etc. Beware of the leaven. A fine place for holding simplicity and emulating faith, that we may not after the manner of the Jews put forth one thing in affection and feign another in voice, since we know that on the day of judgment there can be no hiding-place of fraud.
12.2: 12.2 Nor hidden that shall not be known. Therefore do not imitate the dissemblers, because surely the time will come on the day of judgment in which both your virtue and their hypocrisy will be revealed to all, hence it follows. For what you have said in darkness shall be spoken in the light. Not only in the future will all be plain, but even in the present time in the whole Church throughout the world will be publicly preached what you spoke in darkness, that is in the shadow of pressures and prisons, when your acts shall be read in the highest places. For what you have said in darkness shall be spoken in the light. AMBROSE. What you said in darkness, that is in fear, shall be spoken in light, that is in confidence of truth, the Holy Spirit received. And what in the ear, that is spoken in secret, shall be preached on the housetops, that is the dwelling of the flesh trodden down.
12.4: 12.4 And I say to you. THE SAME. Since the cause of perfidy is twofold, etc., down to so the foundation of faith is fortitude.
12.5: 12.5 But I will show you. Because there are two kinds of persecutors, one openly persecuting, the other craftily flattering. As above against hypocrisy, so here he arms against executioners. This whole place instructs to undergo the passion for the confession of the Lord either by contempt of death, or hope of reward, or in the announcement of punishment for those who remain.
12.6: 12.6 Are not five. AMBROSE. Five sparrows, the five senses of the body; or two according to Matthew, body and soul, etc., down to not doubtful the contemplation of the faithful will avail with him. Sold for a farthing. A dipondius is a weight made of two asses. What in numbers is one, this in weights is an as: what two, this is a dipondius. And one of them, etc. He had inspired the affection of simplicity, raised the courage of the mind, faith alone wavered, this he strengthens from the vilest. As the Apostle says: Does God take care for oxen? 1 Corinthians 9. But care is one thing, knowledge another.
12.7: 12.7 But the very hairs. Not by act of counting but by faculty of knowing, from the likeness of money which is counted to be kept. Where is the great providence of God, that nothing small or idle said escapes him.
